entries.title: White Sox shortstop Colson Montgomery is blunt about offensive struggles — and determined to get past them
entries.summary: <p>Ever gone to the grocery store hungry? Surely everyone has.</p><p>‘‘If you don’t have a plan of what you want to get, you’re gonna [bleeping] go get everything,’’ White Sox shortstop Colson Montgomery said, explaining his recent chasing of pitches out of the strike zone. ‘‘If you have a plan of what you want, you’re probably in and out. That’s what it needs to be for me.’’</p><p>Montgomery hit at an All-Star level for much of the time before the All-Star break but has been struggling offensively for a while now. He drew a walk Tuesday in a six-run first inning the Sox put on potential future Hall of Famer Jacob deGrom and had an RBI single in the fourth, but he entered the night hitting .191/.254/.367 since June 1, even while maintaining a 30-home-run pace.</p><p>Montgomery is coming off a decent road trip (7-for-21, two doubles) that manager Will Venable cited for why he’s close to getting back to being the guy who batted cleanup for the best offense in the American League for much of the season.</p><p>To hear Montgomery tell it, however, that just got him hungry again.</p><p>‘‘Because I saw success, saw results, so I got away from my process,’’ Montgomery told the Sun-Times. ‘‘That leads to chasing results, trying to do too much, trying to go get the game, trying to go get the baseball, rather than just let the game work.”</p><p>In rejecting that Montgomery requires a ‘‘mental break’’ out of the lineup, Venable echoed Sox hitting coaches in praising how the 24-year-old has dealt with his struggles. Teammate Kyle Teel has called him ‘‘one of the best at focusing on the process’’ — and not just because he’s the rare big-leaguer who can conjure relatable grocery-shopping metaphors.</p><p>‘‘Can’t really put words to it, but he’s got that ‘it’ factor,’’ said Rangers first baseman Jake Burger, who trains with Montgomery during the offseason. ‘‘These type of seasons are good for development, trying to figure out how to deal when you’re in a valley and trying to get out as fast as possible.’’</p><p>Regardless, Montgomery’s heady nature hasn’t prevented him from expanding out of the strike zone. His long-limbed swing is geared for power, not average, and elevated strikeout rates are part of the package. But his highs and lows always will be extreme until his rate of swinging at pitches out of the strike zone moves from the top-third of the league to, ideally, the bottom-third.</p><p>Sox hitting coaches have worked to get Montgomery’s long limbs loaded and ready to fire earlier in the opposing pitcher’s motion to give him more time to see and recognize spin. With his injury history, it’s easy to look at his splits since he missed two games in June with tightness in his lower back (.197/.253/.373 with a 37.5% strikeout rate) and wonder whether his daily maintenance of the injury only can accomplish so much. Montgomery, though, points elsewhere.</p><p>‘‘It’s mental,’’ he said. ‘‘If you go up there and you don’t have a plan or a process, [it] doesn’t [bleeping] matter how your body is.’’</p><p>If that’s deflection, it’s deflecting it right onto his own shoulders.</p><p>‘‘I’ve been having really bad decisions at the plate — expanding the zone, making it easy on the pitcher to get me out,’’ he said.</p><p>There are two ways to look at Montgomery’s last three seasons, which have seen long slumps and his prospect status waver but also have come with 48 big-league home runs in 196 career games. Perhaps his game is doomed to swing between extremes, or perhaps he’s a hitter who’s been in this spot before and worked his way out of it.</p><p>‘‘What can we do to make this better?’’ Montgomery said. ‘‘I need to get in the cage. I need to do more decision work. I’ve gotta stay committed to my process, where I’m looking, what is my plan. Having one thought, being as simple as I can. So that’s what I’m trying to do right now.’’</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: After spending last year with champion Dodgers, Michael Conforto eyes doing ‘something special’ with Cubs
entries.summary: <p>PHOENIX – Michael Conforto knows a championship team when he sees one.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ designated hitter and veteran of 11 major league seasons spent last year with the Dodgers, who won their second consecutive World Series.</p><p>Things went well for the Dodgers. They didn’t go so well for Conforto, who didn’t play in the playoffs after hitting .199 during the regular season. But he had a front-row seat to a yearlong championship performance.</p><p>So does he sees any similarities between last year’s Dodgers and this year’s Cubs?</p><p>“I think so,” Conforto said Monday. “I think there’s an expectation. One of the big things is having a real, honest belief that you can win the whole thing, and there’s no doubt we believe that.</p><p>“I don’t think that’s super, super common around the league, to fully, honestly believe that you can win the whole thing. That’s another thing that’s special about this group.”</p><p>The Cubs inked the veteran outfielder in the spring, and he impressed by happily taking on a part-time role.</p><p>“When you sign a player of his stature and they come in and they accept a role that’s not something they’ve done before, it builds things around the room,” manager Craig Counsell said. “Mike’s been a real connector for this group. His production and his leadership from that perspective has been really important.”</p><p>All season long, Conforto has received <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/11/cubs-michael-conforto-stats-lineup-dansby-swanson-craig-counsell-moises-ballesteros" >those kinds of compliments</a> for the part he’s played behind the scenes. The Cubs have cited him as a key ingredient to this year’s mixture, one they hope will yield big things.</p><p>Dodgers-style, championship-type things.</p><p>“I’ve felt more like I’ve come in here and kind of joined the party,” Conforto said. “The big thing is coming in here and being honest: At this point in my career, I just want to win games. That was just a great fit from the beginning.</p><p>“A lot of these guys, maybe it resonated with them that you can get to a place in your career where, maybe, it’s not so much about the money and the playing time and all that stuff but it’s about being a part of something special.</p><p>“I was lucky enough to be somewhat a part of that last year. I just want to do my part to help us get there.”</p><p>But Conforto has been more than just a cheerleader, with vastly better production than what he did in 2025. He came into Tuesday with a .799 OPS that among Cubs hitters trailed only center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong and right fielder Seiya Suzuki.</p><p>Back-to-back games with a home run – including a three-hit effort Monday against the Diamondbacks – helped him break free from a lull at the plate that saw him hit just .145 over 26 games.</p><p>“He’s been incredible on the field, just some of the big, clutch hits he’s had, plus the consistency,” left fielder Ian Happ said Tuesday. “But as a teammate, he’s next level. He’s an all-time teammate.”</p><p>Conforto starts plenty, but he’s shone off the bench, entering Tuesday with a 1.202 OPS and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/24/cubs-michael-conforto-pinch-hit-home-runs-glenallen-hill-nico-hoerner-craig-counsell-gavin-hollowell-hoby-milner-edward-cabrera" >a franchise-record four home runs</a> as a pinch-hitter.</p><p>That’s no small amount of success as the Cubs look forward to the postseason, where having someone like that to call on late in games could perhaps be the difference between advancing to the next round and heading home for the winter.</p><p>Conforto’s seen what makes those sorts of differences. He’s seeing it again with these Cubs.</p><p>“I’ve said quite a bit how committed to winning everybody is here, going the extra mile in everything that they do,” he said. “I’ve been really impressed to see the attention to detail in their routines and how disciplined they’ve been in sticking to everything they’ve been doing since February.</p><p>“It seems to be a culture here, and it makes you want to be a part of the professionalism and the way that everyone goes about their business. That’s one thing that really stands out about this group [when compared to the teams I’ve played for] over the course of my career. There’s a lot of discipline here, and there’s people who really, really want to win.</p><p>“There’s one goal, and it’s winning games.”</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Kevin Gausman shows what he can deliver for Cubs in biggest moments: ‘He’s a huge addition for this team’
entries.summary: <p>PHOENIX – <b>Kevin Gausman</b> was lights out Monday.</p><p>The right-hander showed why he was the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ headlining trade-deadline acquisition with seven shutout innings against a Diamondbacks team that’s been one of baseball’s best since early July.</p><p>It was a solid bounce-back statement in the immediate wake of Gausman failing to make it out of the fifth inning in back-to-back starts.</p><p>Of course, Gausman didn’t need one outing in August to show the Cubs what he’s capable of. He’s been doing big things for a long time, a veteran of 14 major league seasons fresh off a starring role in last year’s postseason, when he put up a 2.93 ERA in six playoff outings, including a pair in the World Series.</p><p>That’s where the Cubs hope to get this fall, and in Gausman, they’ve got someone they believe can help them achieve their championship-level goals.</p><p>“I’m really glad we got Gaus because my numbers against him are terrible,” designated hitter <b>Michael Conforto</b> joked after Monday’s game. “He’s such a good pitcher. He reads swings so well. He has great command. That splitter is devastating. And then he has the postseason pedigree and experience. He knows what those feelings and those situations are like.”</p><p>Conforto didn’t play in last year’s postseason, but he was part of the Dodgers team that edged Gausman’s Blue Jays in the Fall Classic.</p><p>He watched Gausman hold that juggernaut Dodgers lineup to just three runs in a pair of starts, pitching deep into both games, something of a rarity in the all-hands-on-deck world of playoff pitching.</p><p>“I watched the way the Dodgers tried to prepare for him,” Conforto said, “and he diced them up and pitched really well against those guys last year.</p><p>“He’s a huge addition for this team and a great presence.”</p><p>As the Cubs eye a run all the way to the end of October, Gausman is an essential piece of the puzzle.</p><p>“<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/08/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-world-series-blue-jays-yankees-dodgers" >He’s been there and done it</a>,” left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> said Tuesday. “He knows what the emotions are like. He knows how to handle it. He knows what pitching in those moments, in those spots, looks like.</p><p>“As a teammate, you trust the player, because the resume and the back of the baseball card is so impressive.”</p><p>It’s no wonder <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" ><b>Jed Hoyer</b> got aggressive</a> and parted with prospects to add this guy at the deadline.</p><p>“He’s a true pro,” catcher <b>Carson Kelly</b> said. “And he wants the ball. You can see that. Every inning, it seems like he gets stronger and stronger. That’s something that our guys can really look at and build off of.”</p><p><b>PCA oh-fer doesn’t slow Cubs’ offense</b></p><p>For just the third time this season, center fielder <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> had an 0-for-5 night Monday.</p><p>But it didn’t prevent the Cubs from having a big offensive game, scoring seven times.</p><p>It showed there’s plenty more to this lineup beyond the MVP candidate at the top, a preview of how it expects to win in October.</p><p>“They’re just relentless, from 1 through 9,” Gausman said of the Cubs’ lineup. “You try to let up, and then you’ve got a guy like <b>Pedro Ramirez</b> coming up. He’s hitting [close to] .300. There’s no gaps in this lineup.”</p><p>“We can do it in so many different ways,” Happ said, “so you’re not relying on one thing, one person, to get the job done.”</p><p><b>Two-out kings</b></p><p>The Cubs came into Tuesday leading baseball with 274 runs scored and a .757 OPS with two outs.</p><p>A whopping 20 of 26 runs the team scored in blowout wins Sunday and Monday came with two outs.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Two ends of pitching spectrum for Cubs as Clay Holmes dazzles but bullpen stumbles in latest walk-off loss
entries.summary: <p>PHOENIX – For seven innings, Tuesday night looked like a rerun of Monday night’s shutout <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> win.</p><p>By night’s end, it was a rerun of the two walk-off losses the team suffered at the start of their current road trip.</p><p>Righty starter Clay Holmes turned in the Cubs’ second straight stellar effort from a pitcher the team acquired at the trade deadline, matching <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/25/cubs-kevin-gausman-starting-pitching-world-series-playoffs-postseason-michael-conforto-ian-happ-pete-crow-armstrong" >the seven scoreless innings righty Kevin Gausman threw a night earlier</a> and allowing only two hits.</p><p>But the bullpen stumbled, with righty fireballer Daniel Palencia allowing three runs in the eighth inning and righty Jacob Webb giving up a two-out, two-run walk-off homer in the ninth to send the Cubs to a 5-4 defeat against the Diamondbacks, their third walk-off loss in their last five games.</p><p>“I was trying to do my job. It wasn’t my night,” Palencia said after the game. “They beat me today.”</p><p>The D-backs’ rally started frighteningly when Palencia hit outfielder Jordan Lawlar in the helmet with a 98.5 mile an hour pitch. Lawlar fell to the ground as the extended flap that the pitch hit went flying, but he wasn’t down for too long and walked off the field with the trainer.</p><p>Palencia walked the next batter before surrendering a pair of two-out hits, including a fluky double that bounced off first base, exiting with three runs on the board and the Cubs’ lead down to a run.</p><p>“I don’t think it was a bad inning by Danny,” manager Craig Counsell said. “But the bottom line is there were some free passes. Essentially there were two free base-runners with the walk and the hit batter. Then they had some batted-ball luck and a good swing.”</p><p>Webb issued his own walk in the ninth inning before giving up the homer to Ryan Waldschmidt, the second walk-off homer Webb’s allowed in as many outings following a streak of 24 straight scoreless appearances.</p><p>The story changed in a hurry after Holmes picked up where Gausman left off a night earlier, looking the part of a top-of-the-rotation arm as the Cubs steam toward the home stretch of the regular season and the playoffs.</p><p>Jed Hoyer’s front office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >spent prospect capital to land both guys</a>, with Holmes arguably costing the most in the organization’s No. 2-ranked prospect, infielder Jefferson Rojas.</p><p>But the cost has seemed well worth it, as the Cubs look to have two battle-tested veterans they can count on as they plot a run that lasts deep into October.</p><p>“Starting pitchers, you feel what each other do, and when someone else is doing well, you want to take the baton and run with it, really,” Holmes said. “When you have … what Gaus did, what this rotation is capable of doing, you want to follow things up and continue the momentum that’s being built.”</p><p>For all the talk of Gausman’s recent World Series experience – he was strong in the postseason last year, starting twice against the Dodgers – Holmes is only one more year removed from his own Fall Classic success, appearing in all five games of the 2024 Series during his time as the Yankees’ All-Star closer.</p><p>But his move from relief work to starting has gone swimmingly, and the Cubs have a pitcher who’s posted a sparkling 1.96 ERA in his first four outings with his new team.</p><p>“They’re guys that have pitched in big moments, big spots, and that we have a lot of faith in,” said left fielder Ian Happ, who hit a three-run homer Tuesday. “It’s been fun to watch them work.”</p>

entries.title: NIPSCO filed applications for customer rate increases amid storm that ravaged Northwest Indiana
entries.summary: <p>Following a devastating derecho that ravaged Northwest Indiana and left hundreds of thousands without power for two weeks, the Northern Indiana Public Service Company filed documents that would raise electric bills for its customers. </p><p>NIPSCO filed one rate increase application on Aug. 11 — the day of the storms — and two more on Aug. 14 and Aug. 20, respectively, with the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission. </p><p>Together, the totals would amount to a nearly $88 annual increase, and at least partially go into effect as soon as Nov. 1 if approved by state regulators, according to documents filed with the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission.</p><p>In a statement to the Sun-Times Tuesday, NIPSCO said it was “routine” for it to file the requests. In Indiana, utilities can adjust rates biannually or quarterly for certain types of costs. </p><p>The company said it was seeking to “recover” costs for fuel, “regional transmission organization” and “resource adequacy and reliability,” according to filings with the state. Its adjustment for fuel costs asks to “remain in place until replaced by a different fuel cost adjustment that is approved in a subsequent filing.”</p><p>But advocates say the company is out of line, as two weeks after the area was stricken with flooding and 99 mph winds, about 100 customers still remained without power Tuesday evening. The total was down from more than 9,300 on Monday. Initially, nearly 60% of its 500,000 customers were without electricity as 335 damaged poles needed to be repaired or replaced and 27 substations required work.</p><div class="Enhancement" customer bill increase 16.75% in July 2025, or nearly $280 a year, which followed an increase in 2024. The Indiana utility regulation agency’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.in.gov/iurc/files/2026-Electric-Residential-Bill-Survey_Update_7.28.26.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>annual bill survey</u></a> shows that in 2026, the average NIPSCO customer currently pays more than any other Indiana energy customer across all levels of use.</p><p>A recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/23/lawsuit-nipsco-neglected-power-lines-hazard-trees-storms-northwest-indiana-weather-electricity" target="_blank" ><u>class-action lawsuit</u></a> representing several Northwest Indiana residents who were affected during the storm also alleges the utility didn’t protect its power lines from “hazardous trees and other vegetation” near power lines despite customer complaints.</p><p>Indiana Gov. Mike Braun also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/24/indiana-governor-investigation-nipsco-storms-power-outage-gary" target="_blank" ><u>called for an investigation</u></a> into the utility company Monday to “determine whether NIPSCO did what it promised ratepayers and regulators it would do with the money it was given.” He directed the Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor to file a complaint against NIPSCO with the very agency set to hear its case for increasing bills again.</p><p>“NIPSCO is a monopoly utility that Hoosiers pay every month with the expectation that it will use its considerable resources to maintain its system, prepare for severe weather and restore service as quickly as possible when disaster strikes,” Braun said in a statement Sunday. “NIPSCO has failed to keep its end of the bargain.”</p><p>The requests have yet to be ruled on by Indiana's utility board, and utility companies in Illinois have faced pushback for seeking to increase rates. Earlier this year, Peoples Gas proposed a $202 million rate hike, which would bump gas bills by an average of $130 per year. </p><p>But the Illinois attorney general’s office suggested a $4.1 million decrease instead, listing at least $97.2 million in “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/05/06/illinois-attorney-general-kwame-raoul-rate-cut-request-peoples-gas-202m-hike-proposal" >unsupported and unexplained</a>” cost increases for the company’s pipe retirement program, among other “unsubstantiated” charges.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Fiancee Entertains Lawyer With Dishonorable Intentions
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a 63-year-old man. My fiancee (57) and I have been dating exclusively, or so I thought, for four years. I just found out she has a male friend she has been seeing without my knowledge. They go to lunch and dinner and other activities.</p><p>She says they are just friends. He is her attorney, and he wants a romantic relationship. She lied by omission, and now my trust is damaged. I'm worried about her dishonesty and the viability of our relationship. She thinks it's not a big deal. Your thoughts? — <i>SIMMERING SUSPICION IN FLORIDA</i></p><p><b>DEAR SIMMERING SUSPICION:</b> A woman who is engaged has no business spending time alone with another man who has expressed a romantic interest in her. This is a big deal, made bigger by her attempts to hide it and downplay it. Warning: If you go through with this wedding, there's a good chance you'll need to start seeing a lawyer of your own.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I have been married for 34 years. Ten years ago, my husband had to take custody of his then 56-year-old brother, "Clay," because back in 1987 he fried his brain on PCP. For a decade, our life has been a daily living hell.</p><p>Clay has frightened off one of our cats. He lies, steals from us, can't and won't clean up after himself and doesn't wash his hands. He is the most disgusting person I have ever met. He's spoiled rotten and lazy and expects the only woman in the home to do everything. This is an ingrained behavior that he has had for years.</p><p>I want a divorce. My husband will not put Clay into an assisted living facility or a mental institution. I love my husband, but I refuse to be disrespected by anyone. I told him I wouldn't ever allow any member of my family to disrespect him the way I, our marriage and our home have been disrespected by his brother. Abby, would you divorce your husband for subjecting you to this daily living hell for 10 years? — <i>DONE IN MONTANA</i></p><p><b>DEAR DONE:</b> I certainly wouldn't have put up with your mess of a brother-in-law for an entire decade! Still, if you are considering divorce, you must mention that to your husband. Offer him a final opportunity to make other arrangements for his brother. Be clear that if he continues to value Clay's comfort over yours, the marriage is over.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a boy in South Korea who likes boys. When I was in middle school, I loved girls just like everyone else, but it changed after entering high school. When I see boys in school now, I have started to feel the charm of them. These days, I'm scared that if I reveal it, I'll be mocked by my friends and others. What should I do? — <i>NOT STRAIGHT IN SEOUL, S. KOREA</i></p><p><b>DEAR NOT STRAIGHT:</b> If you don't feel comfortable or safe coming out to your friends, it's OK to wait. All of this gets a bit easier after you graduate, especially if you are able to attend a university. For now, focus on your studies so you can make that happen. To find gay or gay-friendly people to talk to outside your school, look up an organization called Dding Dong at ddingdong.kr.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned the column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Northwestern must elevate — not retreat from — African studies program
entries.summary: <p>In 1948, when most American universities barely regarded Africa as worthy of sustained scholarly attention, Northwestern University took a visionary step by creating the country's first <a class="Link" href="https://africanstudies.northwestern.edu/" target="_blank" >program of African studies. </a></p><p>The program’s founder, anthropologist Melville J. Herskovits, devoted his career to challenging the assumption that Africa existed only as a footnote in Western history. He argued that the people and cultures of African descent must be understood on their own terms — not through the distortions of colonial prejudice. He also insisted that Black American culture was neither deficient nor “pathological” but deeply rooted in African histories and traditions. </p> <p>For nearly 80 years, Northwestern celebrated that intellectual audacity as evidence of its global leadership and moral seriousness. Yet at the very moment the university is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/9/28/23377919/northwestern-football-stadium-ryan-field-evanston" >showcasing</a> its privately funded <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2025/07/30/northwestern-ryan-field-wildcats-mark-jackson-david-braun-evanston-big-ten-college-football" >$850 million-plus</a> new football stadium, it appears to be preparing to diminish the African studies program, an institution that helped propel Northwestern's rise as an academic behemoth.</p><p>The contrast is difficult to ignore. Universities are entitled to make choices. But when a university can find the money for athletics while reducing support for the African studies program, it is also making a statement about what it values, what it wishes to be known for and what parts of its inheritance it is willing to leave behind.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ee0000" name="module-ee0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>University officials have been countering recent reports of the program's imminent demise. The program, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/16/northwestern-says-african-studies-not-closing-staff-told-otherwise" >according to a spokesperson</a>, has not closed but is “transitioning away from” its status as a universitywide research institute and center.</p><p>Staff have said otherwise. They were told they would no longer be employed as of Aug. 31.</p><p>The conflicting messages have left faculty, alumni, donors and international partners uncertain about what will remain and what will be lost.</p><p>The most important question is not whether African studies survives on paper but whether Northwestern is weakening its commitment to it.</p><p>Institutions can't communicate its priorities through news releases. They need to be conveyed through investment, staffing, organizational support and tangible commitments. Simply preserving the program’s name while reducing staff, resources and institutional standing signals that African studies is no longer welcome in a space of prominence.</p><p>Africa is home to the world’s youngest population, some of its fastest-growing economies and extraordinary innovation in technology, entrepreneurship, public health, culture and governance. If ever there were a moment for universities to deepen their engagement with Africa, it is now. Northwestern should be leading that effort.</p><p>Instead, it appears to be stepping back, shirking its role as a university that has cultivated international research partnerships, trained distinguished scholars and developed the premier <a class="Link" href="https://www.library.northwestern.edu/libraries-collections/distinctive-special-collections/herskovits-library/" target="_blank" >Melville J. Herskovits Library of African Studies</a>.</p><p>Building on those accomplishments is the only way to move forward instead of speaking of them as triumphs of the past. </p><p>Celebrating Northwestern's historic feats in fundraising campaigns and admissions materials isn't enough. That history must be strengthened and protected.</p><p>The issue before Northwestern is not an accounting exercise. It is a test of institutional character at a time when the Trump administration is blocking or whitewashing classroom lessons and public displays about systemic racism and slavery. </p><p>Those who care about the university’s future should not remain silent. Alumni, students, faculty, donors and trustees should demand Northwestern leadership offer a clear commitment to the future of African studies with dedicated staffing, stable funding and an ambitious vision worthy of the program’s historic reputation and status.</p><p>Preservation alone shows weak-kneed leadership. </p><p>The university that pioneered African studies in America should not be asking how little support it can provide while still claiming the program survives. It should be asking how it can expand a legacy that has distinguished Northwestern for nearly eight decades.</p><p>At a moment when Africa’s economic, political, cultural and demographic significance to the world has never been greater, retreat is the wrong message from an institution that once led the way.</p><p>The new Ryan Field will eventually grow old. A decision that could gut the African studies program will also age, but not in the way Northwestern would like to be remembered: standing on the wrong side of history. </p><p><i>Dr. Jeffrey Sterling, a Northwestern University alum, is the author of the book "Voices and Visions: The Evolution of the Black Experience at Northwestern University." He was the president of Northwestern University's Black Alumni Association from 2014-2018.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9e0000" name="module-9e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Asif Amin Cheema's deportation demonstrates cruelty of U.S.
entries.summary: <p>WBEZ's Esther Yoon-Ji Kang's article on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/08/21/deported-operation-midway-blitz-asif-amin-cheema-pakistan-best-sub-humboldt-park-addison" >Asif Amin Cheema’s</a> deportation was absolutely heartbreaking. I can't understand why anyone would think deporting this gentleman was the right thing to do. No one is made safer by this, and no one’s life is made better. Instead, a family is torn to shreds, a young man’s life is made substantially more difficult, and a good father is exiled to a country he barely knows anymore. This is simply cruelty for the sake of cruelty, and the infliction of pain for the sake of inflicting pain. </p><p>How can rational, fair-minded people think to themselves, "Yes, great, this is what I want my federal government to do, and this is how I want my country to treat people?"</p><p>What has happened to basic notions of kindness and decency? What has happened to my country?</p><p><i>Andy Boyd, Wheaton</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3e0000" name="module-3e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Divulge data centers’ environmental impact </h3><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/11/mayor-brandon-johnson-chicago-moratorium-data-centers-new-regulations" >call for a temporary moratorium</a> on new and expanded data centers in Chicago is a sign Illinois can't ignore the environmental and infrastructure demands of this rapidly growing industry. But the call should also prompt a broader question: How can Illinois make informed decisions about data center growth when it does not have data on how much water and electricity these facilities use?</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoisedc.org/news/illinois-excels-as-top-5-global-data-center-destination/" target="_blank" >Chicago area</a> is already the third-largest data center market in the country and fourth-largest globally. As artificial intelligence accelerates demand for computing power, that growth is likely to continue. Data centers can require enormous amounts of electricity and water to operate and cool their servers. Some facilities can consume <a class="Link" href="https://www.eesi.org/articles/view/data-centers-and-water-consumption" target="_blank" >millions of gallons</a> of water per day.</p><p>There is no question data centers <a class="Link" href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/new-evidence-on-data-center-employment-effects/" target="_blank" ><u>create jobs</u></a>, attract investment and help keep our state competitive in the technology industry. But economic growth should not come at the expense of transparency.</p><p>That transparency was offered in the proposed <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus/FullText?LegDocId=210137&DocName=10400SB2181sam001&DocNum=2181&DocTypeID=SB&LegID=161884&GAID=18&SessionID=114&SpecSess=&Session=" target="_blank" >Illinois Data Center Energy and Water Reporting Act</a>, which would require data centers to annually report their water and energy consumption. Unfortunately, the legislation <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocTypeID=SB&DocNum=2181&GAID=18&SessionID=114&LegID=161884" target="_blank" >stalled in committee</a>. </p><p>Chicago’s new regulatory measures show that concerns about data centers are growing. But local action isn't enough. <a class="Link" href="https://www.epa.gov/power-sector/emissions-monitoring-and-reporting" target="_blank" >Power plants</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://epa.illinois.gov/topics/drinking-water/field-operations/daily-operating-reports.html" target="_blank" >water utilities</a> already report environmental information. Data centers aren’t any different. The public has a right to know how shared resources are being used.</p><p>Illinois may ultimately decide that the economic benefits of data center growth outweigh its demands on our water and energy infrastructure. But that decision should be based on reliable data, not assumptions. </p><p><i>Emma Lu, Buffalo Grove</i></p><h3>Outcomes-based training is win for ex-offenders, taxpayers </h3><p>While I generally consider myself “tough on crime," Uzoma “Zo” Orchingwa’s recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/08/19/prison-ex-offender-job-training-safety-costs-chicago-uzoma-zo-orchingwa" >op-ed</a> on modifying vocational training for ex-offenders by including some compensation upon verification of their training achievements makes sense. Recidivism <a class="Link" href="https://worldpopulationreview.com/state-rankings/recidivism-rates-by-state" target="_blank" >statistics</a> suggest that most of the formerly incarcerated want to get back into the legitimate working world.</p><p>A few years ago, I had my car towed from the Eisenhower Expressway. Riding to the repair shop, the tow-truck driver shared how he had been released from prison years ago after shooting and wounding a rival gang member.</p><p>The man told me he had a wife, children and close friends and that he helped support his local church. He wasn't 100% sure if he had been taught how to earn a commercial driver’s license and operate a truck at a much earlier age, if his life would be that much different, but he believed he might never had “held a gun."</p><p>Some deserve imprisonment. Yet, upon release, people should be given a meaningful opportunity to prove their worth to the community. Closely monitored, incentivized job training may not only save taxpayers money but also save lives.</p><p><i>Terry Takash, Western Springs</i></p><h3>Keep focus on American’s detention in China </h3><p>I'm pleased I had to withdraw the op-ed I submitted against the U.S. State Department's seeming passivity on China's arrest and detention of American citizen Min Zin and the lassitude of the U.S. media toward the scholar's plight.</p><p>Last week, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/20/us/politics/scholar-china-wrongfully-detained.html" target="_blank" >State Department </a>designated Min Zin as “wrongfully detained” and formally called on China for his release. The New York Times gave this <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/20/us/politics/scholar-china-wrongfully-detained.html" target="_blank" >news</a> prominence. I found some hope with both actions. </p><p>The State Department's designation suggests a solution is at hand, especially with the White House preparing to welcome President Xi Jinping next month.</p><p>In my op-ed, I had argued that even in a news environment filled with complex crises, the long, harrowing struggle of Myanmar’s citizens against vicious usurpers deserves prime time. Perhaps that time is now, as Min Zin needs ongoing support and coverage.</p><p>Born in Myanmar, he was, from an early age, committed to replace a cruel junta with a democratic government. At 14, he attended his first <a class="Link" href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2022/01/28/myanmar-year-brutality-coups-wake" target="_blank" >peaceful demonstration</a>. The military, noting his participation, ordered him expelled from school.</p><p>When he persisted over the years, he was harassed. Finally, when armed soldiers threatened his family, he fled, first to Thailand, then to the United States, where he studied political science at University of California Berkeley. (His pending Ph.D. dissertation concerns the civil-military relations and political transition in Myanmar.)</p><p>As the press for democracy continued, Min Zin paid heed. In 2016, he established the <a class="Link" href="https://ispmyanmar.com/about/" target="_blank" >Institute for Strategy and Policy — Myanmar</a> think tank considered <a class="Link" href="https://english.dvb.no/us-citizen-and-prominent-myanmar-analyst-min-zin-arrested-in-china-on-national-security-charges/" target="_blank" >to be among the most respected academic authorities</a> on the complex geopolitical ties between Beijing and Naypyidaw, the administrative capital of Myanmar.</p><p>When the military executed <a class="Link" href="https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/3/27/who-is-fighting-in-myanmars-multi-front-civil-war" target="_blank" >a vicious coup in 2021</a>, throwing the country into civil war, Min Zin worked from Thailand, where he could continue research.</p><p>He does not belong in jail. He belongs in headlines. I trust Americans will be enthusiastic about the State Department support and will continue to engage and press for his freedom.</p><p><i>Susanne Dumbleton, professor emeritus, DePaul University</i><br></p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams' up-and-down camp continues, but coach Ben Johnson 'happy' with is progress
entries.summary: <p>The public confidence in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> starts with trust in coach Ben Johnson. And Johnson is asking for some of that trust right now.</p><p>Williams was unremarkable in his preseason debut and hasn’t blown anyone away with his training camp so far. None of it has been alarming, but it hasn’t been definitively reassuring, either.</p><p>Johnson clearly has grown tired of the topic, and questions about it have annoyed him the last few days.</p><p>When he was asked why he played Williams and the other offensive starters in the preseason game against the Bengals, Johnson’s first reaction was, ‘‘OK,’’ before resetting and repeating a line about assessing the workload and concluding with, ‘‘We felt like we needed this work.’’</p><p>He smiled and exhaled in the middle of a question when he was asked Tuesday about things he would like to see Williams clean up to be game-ready by the regular-season opener Sept. 13 at the Panthers.</p><p>‘‘I’ve been pretty consistent that I’m happy with where he’s at,’’ Johnson said before practice. ‘‘I love the approach that he takes coming in to work every day. I love his demeanor on the field. There’s a level of professionalism that radiates from him. Everything he’s doing . . . there’s a mission in mind, so I appreciate that about him.’’</p><p>Johnson then pivoted into more of an actual to-do list that included sharper passing in two-minute drills and acknowledged it has been ‘‘a little bit of a mixed bag over the last few weeks’’ for the first-team offense. He also wants better recognition and anticipation of defensive coverages from Williams and said he challenged him on that Monday.</p><p>Training camp is long for everyone, and the spotlight is always on Williams. Johnson’s standard is what matters most at Halas Hall, and he’s sick of answering questions based on someone else’s grading scale.</p><p>But this is part of Williams not only being the face of the franchise but also being anointed as one of the NFL’s next big stars with a Madden cover, the No. 51 spot in the player-voted rankings and outsized national media attention.</p><p>Also, if he had been overwhelming and had cleared the very high bar of expectations entering his third season, the questions would be different. He still is riding potential at the moment, and that too often has been a route with no destination for Bears quarterbacks.</p><p>Williams got better last season, but that wasn’t an arrival. He and Johnson both have said it.</p><p>He made flat-out spectacular plays, but he finished last in completion percentage (58.1), second-to-last in on-target throws (69.8%, according to Pro Football Reference) and 22nd in passer rating (90.1). He had three games in the second half of the season in which he threw for fewer than 200 yards.</p><p>Johnson needs him to boost all those numbers by being more of a technician, which is why he hasn’t let up on his mandate that Williams complete 70% of his passes. Otherwise, the Bears aren’t getting everything they can out of the offensive mastermind they hired.</p><p>Williams had another nondescript practice Tuesday. He threw incomplete on five of six passes during a seven-on-seven period, though one of those was a drop by running back D’Andre Swift and another was a deep heave out of the back of the end zone when none of his reads materialized.</p><p>He had two sharp passes to wide receiver Rome Odunze, one a 30-yarder over the middle and another in the back of the end zone during a red-zone period.</p><p>Williams got three possessions in the red zone, all starting at the 14-yard line: the touchdown pass to Odunze, a touchdown run by Swift from the 14 and a third-down pass to Odunze that linebacker Devin Bush deflected.</p><p>Behind Williams, the Bears got backup quarterback Tyson Bagent back on the field for the first time since he hurt his hamstring in the preseason opener against the Browns, though third-stringer Case Keenum also took some of the second-team snaps.</p><p>Williams hasn’t been available to the media this week and probably won’t be until after the Bears’ joint practice Thursday with the Titans. But coming out of the joint practice and preseason game against the Bengals, he described last week similar to how Johnson did.</p><p>He saw explosive plays but also some flat-lining. There were penalties and a fumbled snap. The two-minute drill at the end Thursday slammed to a halt when he threw an interception under pressure.</p><p>The offense can’t continue to be ‘‘a mixed bag’’ if the Bears are going to contend this season. There must be some leveling out, and that — like everything else on that side of the ball — starts with Williams.</p><p>That responsibility is greater because of uncertainty about the Bears’ defense and their offensive line. They might not survive without Williams lighting up the scoreboard, and he’ll be forced to operate much faster if the line isn’t as sturdy as it was last season.</p><p>The upside for him is that Johnson is the one illuminating the path forward, rather than the clumsy guidance Williams got as a rookie under Matt Eberflus and Shane Waldron, and things can change quickly in camp. Sometimes something just clicks and it all looks right.</p><p>Johnson seems sure it’s headed that way and, after his success last season, has the credibility to say that — even if it doesn’t seem that way to everyone else. But the Bears will dive into the season soon, and everyone will be grading Williams on the same criteria at that point.</p>

entries.title: Review: “Adolescent Salvation” at Theater Wit
entries.summary: <p>Have you eavesdropped on the conversation of a high school girl lately? I have. And let me tell you, the content of these chats will make your head spin.</p><p>So, when playwright Tim Venable stages a pivot in the open of “Adolescent Salvation” from three teens at a sleepover silently scrolling social media, to one complaining about boredom, to another casually telling a friend to kill herself in response — he totally captures the essence of present day teens. It’s morbid. And unsettling. Venable and Cienfuegos have found the sweet spot of capturing the full Gen Z aesthetic without falling into the trap of cringy generalizations or the overuse of internet slang.</p><p>The production will still be a bit jarring for those unfamiliar with the lives of present day teens. While the time period is the now, the overall feel harkens back to sex, drugs and rock-and-roll (or in this case, Taylor Swift).</p><p>The audience is immediately transported into the world of 15-year-old loner Natasha (Piper Jean Bailey) through excellent stage design by Jonathan Berg-Einhorn. The audience enters the theater through Natasha’s closet, literally walking through her hanging garments to get to seats.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.0" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> “Adolescent Salvation” </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fa0000" name="module-fa0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">“Adolescent Salvation”</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When: </b>through Oct. 3<br><b>Where: </b>Theater Wit, 1229 W. There’s no separation between Natasha’s space and the audience. The theater is immersed in her room, with seating replacing each wall. There are moments in the production where characters are face-to-face with audience members as they deliver lines from Natasha’s desk. This creates the feeling that we are all in the action, of which this production has plenty, and this stage design makes the disquieting scenes feel inescapable. It’s clever and makes the set a key component to the success of the production.</p><p>This is a dark comedy, with emphasis on the dark. I don’t want to spoil a major plot point, but when this play takes a turn from mean-spirited sleepover to <i>OMG what the hell is going on</i> — the only comparison I can give (without spoiling) is And not like a car-crash can’t look away, but deep uncomfortability. I kept wondering how far this team of actors could take it (and it goes farther than I would have liked). Yet, it is well deserving of a positive review because the production pulls this off effectively. My personal difficulty is how to properly explain all of this without spoiling a plot point the production clearly wants to keep. The producers even go so far as not mentioning one of the characters in any of the promotional materials, including web and playbill.</p><p>Here is what I can say. Bailey is captivating as Natasha, the teen whose family life is blown up after her father had an affair and ran off with another woman. In the opening scenes, it’s immediately clear Bailey is playing a role that is younger than she is, and her tone of voice while conveying youthfulness is a little distracting. Later, after the reveal, it becomes appreciated.</p><p>Natasha is joined in her sleepover by Taylor (Jordan Levene), whose mother is at Margaritaville with Natasha’s mom, and Taylor’s best friend, also named Taylor (Brandon Acosta) who tags along. They are teens, so of course they steal booze from Natasha’s mom, smoke weed and talk about crushes.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The arc of Jordan Leven’s Taylor is one of the play’s many surprises. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Boris Martin</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>This play has a ton of turns and surprises. One of my favorites is the arc of Leven’s Taylor. Early, she’s pegged as a Regina George-style mean girl, but by the end her use of ferociousness transforms from sharp verbal jabs and coercion to friendship and an act of valiance.</p><p>Thematically, the play takes a shift in the third act that teeters slapstick. It’s awkwardly sandwiched between teens trying to solve an unsolvable problem and a solemn (and perhaps unnecessary) moment between a drunk mother and her curious daughter. It shouldn’t work, but in the context of the presented circumstances, it serves as a well-received palate cleanser.</p><p>It also ties this production together. This play is <i>messy</i>. It captures teenage angst while ratcheting the stakes to levels unimaginable to most viewers. Then, the first act villain becomes a hero and the shy and reserved girl discovers her power while utilizing tequila the way Popeye uses spinach. The ups and downs and changes in tone feel genuinely reflective of what it feels like to be a teenage girl: scary.</p>

entries.title: ‘American Doctor’ highlights story of Chicago physician fighting for Palestinians in Gaza and back home
entries.summary: <p>As the father of two young daughters, Dr. Thaer Ahmad sees his own children when he treats Palestinians wounded in the Israel-Hamas war.</p><p>“I’m a Palestinian who wants to see babies that look like my babies not be killed anymore,” he says in the new documentary, “American Doctor,” which opens this week in Chicago.</p><p>The film, directed by Malaysian-born, New York-based Poh Si Teng, follows three American doctors who have gone on international humanitarian missions, visiting 10 different countries over the years.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div hospitals in Gaza both before and after the initial ceasefire. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Watermelon Pictures</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“I used to work for Al Jazeera and it was a year into the genocide, and seeing so many of my former colleagues being targeted and executed,” Teng said in a Zoom interview of what prompted her to make her first feature-length documentary.</p><p>“People were silent and still whispering about Palestinian colleagues and our peers getting killed when they had no issue at all talking about Ukrainian journalists or American journalists who were kidnapped in Ukraine or killed by Russia,” she observed.</p><p>Teng pivoted from documenting reporters in Gaza to physicians. “Americans love medical dramas. I love medical dramas. And I definitely love ‘The Pitt.’ I thought to myself, We're gonna make ‘The Pitt.’ It's gonna be real, and it's gonna be set in Gaza.”</p><p>“As a filmmaker, I'm not a doctor,” added Teng. “I can't save lives. I can just tell a story.”</p><p>“American Doctor” opens with a chaotic scene of a 10-year-old girl rushed into Nasser Medical Complex in the Gaza Strip after an Apache helicopter attack. In the next scene, Dr. Mark Perlmutter, one of Teng’s three subjects, insists the director not blur the faces of six dead babies in a photograph. Later the North Carolina orthopedic and hand surgeon vents: “I'm sorry but the rate of killing of children in Gaza is six hundred times higher than it is in Ukraine. This is sick.”</p><p>The film chronicles the doctors’ work in the field, including at Nasser when Israeli projectiles strike, killing patients — even the hospital’s sign takes a direct hit. Most Gaza medical buildings are reportedly in ruins.</p><p>The documentary also follows the doctors speaking in diverse forums. At a wintry Chicago rally, Ahmad talks about the stories of people who are killed that go untold. “I see pictures of the journalists that have been killed. I see pictures of the children that have been killed. It's on us to make sure that their stories are told, because if you turn on the news right now, you will not hear anything about them.” </p><p>The doctors also visit congressional offices and testify before the United Nations in the film. In one scene, Ahmad testifies: “I say this as a Palestinian who yesterday had to watch a mother say that she found the body of her child outside of their house but could not find his head and spent the entire night with a flashlight going through the streets, roaming through the streets of Khan Yunis, hoping to find his head but being unsuccessful.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> He graduated from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and received his medical degree from Rush Medical College. He currently serves as a clinical assistant professor in the Department of Emergency Medicine at the University of Illinois Chicago. </p><p>In a Zoom interview, Ahmad said his father immigrated to Chicago to study electrical engineering at the Illinois Institute of Technology. At age 5 he made his first of many trips to the Middle East to visit grandparents in a Jerusalem suburb. His first NGO medical mission to the Gaza Strip was in 2009. </p><p>Ahmad told the Sun-Times he spoke out at a 2010 memorial in Grant Park for young Palestinian victims of an IDF operation: “We got together and we got 300 black balloons that signified all of the kids that had been killed. And we released these balloons.”</p><p>Pro-Palestinian protests are a family tradition. “After Sept. 11th and especially during the invasion of Iraq in 2003, every Friday me and my parents (and his three siblings) would hop on buses from Little Palestine, head to the city, and participate in these protests in downtown Chicago.” Ahmad and his wife now take their two daughters to marches. </p><p>Near the end of “American Doctor” Ahmad flies to Amman, Jordan. For the fifth time, Israeli authorities block him from crossing the border. As the sun sets he holds up his phone so his family back home can see what he sees. Afterward, he turns to the camera and says: “I have a 5-year-old daughter. In five years, she's going to ask me: ‘What was this genocide that happened? And what did you do?’”</p><p><i>On a six-city tour, Po and Ahmad will appear for a Q/A at a special screening at 6:30 p.m. Aug. 26 at the Music Box Theater, 3733 N. Southport Ave. Doctors, nurses, EMTs and medical students can get complimentary tickets at </i><a class="Link" href="http://www.watermelon.pics/adhealthcare" target="_blank" ><i><u>watermelon.pics/adhealthcare</u></i></a><i>.</i></p><p><i>“American Doctor” opens on Aug. 28 at the Gene Siskel Film Center, 164 N. State St., and Uprising Theater & Cafe, 2905 N. Milwaukee. On Sept. 4 the documentary moves to The Wilmette Theatre at 1122 Central Ave., Wilmette. On Sept. 11 it will screen at Alamo Drafthouse Wrigleyville, 3519 N. Clark St.</i></p>

entries.title: Blue Cross Blue Shield lowers payment for therapists, pediatricians under new ‘downcoding’ policy
entries.summary: <p>The day a Chicago woman named Rachel learned Blue Cross Blue Shield of Illinois was "downcoding" her longtime psychiatrist’s claims and cutting his pay, she immediately got to work.</p><p>She reached out to elected and state officials to see what, if anything, could be done to reverse the insurance company’s new policy that left her psychiatrist getting paid so little for each visit that he was considering dropping her insurance entirely.</p><p>“I’m going to do absolutely everything I can do to avenge my wonderful psychiatrist,” said Rachel, who asked to withhold her last name out of fear that speaking out could negatively impact her professionally.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-hangLeft> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Rachel has been reaching out to public officials about the reduced pay her doctor is getting as a result of automatic ‘downcoding’ of insurance claims by Blue Cross Blue Shield and other health insurers.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>As of July 1, Blue Cross Blue Shield changed the way it evaluates some medical claims that health professionals regularly submit, resulting in lower payment for the same service than in the past, according to mental health clinicians, doctors and advocates who spoke to the Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ. Providers can appeal each decreased claim, but many say that’s too burdensome given the large volume of impacted claims. They worry the financial hit they are experiencing could lead to reduced patient access or even affect their ability to retain staff.</p><p>This downcoding trend has become so common among health insurers that state lawmakers passed a law in July to prohibit these automatic reductions in reimbursements. But it doesn't go into effect until 2028.</p><p>The BCBS claims at the center of this change are for the “bread and butter” codes physicians use for reimbursement, said Stephen Gillaspy, deputy chief for health policy and healthcare financing at the American Psychological Association. These are for visits that insurance companies consider to be part of “evaluation and management services.”</p><p>“If you call your primary care doc and say you’re feeling sick and you go in, they’re going to bill you for an [evaluation and management services] code,” Gillaspy said.</p><p>But earlier this year, BCBS announced on its <a class="Link" href="https://www.bcbsil.com/provider/education/education-reference/news/2026/3-16-2026-claim-editing-changes-for-evaluation-and-management-services" target="_blank" ><u>website</u></a>, “When we review your claim for dates of service beginning July 1, if services billed do not support the level of E&M services billed, your reimbursement will be for a lower level of service validated.”</p><p>In a statement, BCBS defended the change in how it’s processing claims, saying it is committed to “expanding access to quality health care.”</p><p>“Our enhanced claims review process is well designed and intended to appropriately support accurate payments of correctly coded claims for the level of service that was provided,” the company said.</p><p>Most clinicians submit claims for evaluation and management services, but providers in the Chicago area say they are seeing a trend of BCBS automatically decreasing claims for specific kinds of visits — ones involving more complex cases or longer visits. So far, providers are reporting this most acutely in mental health and pediatric practices, according to medical professional organizations.</p><p>Many wonder if the change is driven by an artificial intelligence tool because of how many claims are downcoded in bulk. BCBS did not comment on whether it was using an AI tool.</p><p>Dr. Josh Levin, a suburban pediatrician, said about 40% of claims for higher level sick visits at his practice were downcoded in recent weeks by BCBS, resulting in lower payments. This is unsustainable, he said, and could eventually lead to access issues if they can’t afford to hire more doctors.</p><p>One Chicago practice that includes psychiatrists and psychotherapists had 2,400 claims reduced out of the blue by BCBS in July alone, according to one psychiatrist. He asked not to be identified out of concern it could negatively impact the practice.</p><p>It’s routine for BCBS to audit the practice’s claims but that’s not what led to the reduced claims, the psychiatrist said. During an audit, the insurer typically reviews records provided by the practice to back up why they bill under certain codes. But he and others say Blue Cross Blue Shield never reviewed records or requested additional documentation.</p><p>“For patients that we have been billing the same code for the past five years, all of a sudden Blue Cross Blue Shield is saying ‘We’re not going to pay you for that code, we’re going to pay you for a code that reimburses at a lower dollar amount,’” the psychiatrist said.</p><h3>New state law aimed at preventing downcoding</h3><p>This change comes as Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker signed into law the <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/PublicActs/View/104-0568" target="_blank" ><u>Transparency in Downcoding Act</u></a>, which is meant to limit what doctors and experts say is a growing problem among a range of insurance companies.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://healthnewsillinois.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Downcoding-Survey-Report-FINAL.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>survey</u></a> from the Illinois State Medical Society earlier this year found that 72% of medical practices had experienced automatic downcoding and underpayment by insurers.</p><p>Illinois’ new <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus/FullText?GAID=18&DocNum=3114&DocTypeID=SB&LegId=165735&SessionID=114" target="_blank" ><u>law</u></a> prohibits health insurers from using an automated process, such as with artificial intelligence or an algorithm, to determine if claims submitted by doctors or physician assistants should be reduced. It also ensures doctors are notified when a claim has been downcoded and reimbursed at a lower level, and prevents downcoding to discriminate against doctors who regularly treat patients with complex or chronic conditions.</p><p>But the law, which doesn’t go into effect until 2028, doesn’t protect all medical providers, said Julietta Mkrtychian, chief of staff for state Rep. Lindsey LaPointe, a Chicago Democrat.</p><p>“The bill itself isn’t going to be the thing that saves all the providers from our insurance companies’ bad behavior,” Mkrtychian said. “We definitely have to think more expansively.”</p><p>State lawmakers may have to consider passing another bill, she said, or potentially look to the Illinois Department of Insurance for help in instances of downcoding.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7f0000" name="image-7f0000"></a> & Wellness in Chicago. There’s a limited number of prescribing psychologists who practice psychotherapy, do psychological testing and prescribe certain medications for people with a range of mental health conditions, from anxiety to schizophrenia. In recent weeks he’s had dozens of his claims reduced by Blue Cross Blue Shield, which means both he and the practice he works for earn less for the same amount of work.</p><p>The small practice likely won’t be able to tackle appealing each downcoded claim, especially because each one is assessed individually.</p><p>“We only get paid based on what we’re reimbursed by insurance companies,” Phillips said. “So if they pay less, we make less.”</p><h3>‘It’s a huge access issue’</h3><p>For some doctors, the financial cost of Blue Cross Blue Shield’s decision to downgrade claims and lower reimbursement rates may be too much to bear. And it comes when finding a therapist is already a struggle for many people.</p><p>Rachel, the Chicago patient with BCBS insurance, said her psychiatrist informed her and his other patients that he doesn’t think he can continue with BCBS patients as long as the policy is in effect.</p><p>She is willing to pay for her visits, even at nearly $200 per session. She usually sees her psychiatrist twice a year.</p><p>“I’m going to pay out of pocket to see him because I can,” Rachel said. “And I have no intention of finding another psychiatrist that doesn’t have years and years of my personal relationship with them. entries.title: Why is the island in Washington Park behind a locked gate?
entries.summary: <p>On a recent day, Jonathan Schlesinger took a walk through Washington Park on Chicago’s South Side. He works for the Illinois Department of Natural Resources, and he was scoping out the lagoon for a fishing event. A couple of bridges cross the water to a roughly 9-acre piece of land called Bynum Island. When Schlesinger walked across one, a tall metal fence stopped him. He wondered why the island was gated off and if this “lost world” would ever be open to the public.</p><p>Bynum Island has been closed to the public for years, but back in the 1970s, it buzzed with children enjoying a Space Age playground. Several decades before that, the island served as a holding pen for sheep that grazed in Washington Park.</p><p>Today, people still sneak onto the island, sometimes to bird-watch, other times for less innocent activities. It didn’t include an island — it was a peninsula sticking out into the water. The architects envisioned it as a paddock where deer would live.</p><p>In their plan, <a class="Link" href="https://hdl.handle.net/2027/loc.ark:/13960/t24b3kp1n?urlappend=%3Bseq=28" target="_blank" ><u>Olmsted and Vaux explained</u></a> that the deer would be “confined by an under-water fence, as it is not safe for deer to range where there are children.” This spit of land did not actually end up serving as a deer paddock, said Julia Bachrach, who worked for 29 years as the Chicago Park District’s historian. But the park did have deer and sheep during its early history.</p><p>Olmsted and Vaux wanted the park to be pastoral — a restful place where city residents would feel calm as they watched animals grazing, Bachrach explained.</p><p>Bigger than downtown’s Grant Park, Washington Park covers more than 300 acres, stretching from 51st Street to 60th Street, from Cottage Grove Avenue to King Drive. But in the original 1871 plan, it was part of an even more expansive green space, extending across what was then Chicago’s southern outskirts. Over time, Olmsted and Vaux’s plan evolved into three parks: Jackson Park, the Midway Plaisance and Washington Park.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" In the early 2000s, it was occasionally opened up for an adventure fitness program using an obstacle course. Schlesinger’s Curious City question, I slipped through a gap in Bynum Island’s fence on a spring day, seeking out a worm-eating warbler, a bird species rarely seen in Chicago. On the island, I came across the amphitheater’s stone circle and pieces of the obstacle course, identified by old signs as a squeeze box, a tunnel, an incomplete bridge and something called a “wobbly woozy.”</p><p>I’m not the only birder who has ventured into this forbidden zone. Cody Paulsen, the first birder who’d spotted the worm-eating warbler, said the island attracts many migratory species. “What I like the most about birding is that it’s taken me a lot of places, both within the city and elsewhere, that I never would have gone before,” he said. “I think there’s a lot of places in Chicago, especially on the South Side, that are underrepresented or undersurveyed. I mean, really, when you think of Bynum Island, the sky is almost the limit.”</p><p>The Chicago Park District has been working on a new framework plan for improvements in Washington Park. entries.title: One of the Shedd’s rescued beluga whales has died
entries.summary: <p><i>This is a developing story; check back for updates. </i></p><p>One of eight Shedd Aquarium beluga whales recently rescued from a shuttered aquatic park in Canada has died, the aquarium announced Wednesday.</p><p>Peekachu, a 23-year-old female beluga, arrived at Shedd with three others about two weeks ago.</p><p>“In the days that followed the rescue, Peekachu showed early signs of progress as she ate squid, herring and capelin from caretakers and checked out the care team from the underwater windows as they monitored the progress of the rescues,” Shedd said in a statement. “Yesterday, we got an opportunity to get blood samples from Peekachu, who was not consistently eating her full diet. When we looked at the blood values, we were concerned that she was dehydrated and needed supportive care. On Tuesday evening, as teams worked to provide her with medicine and fluids, Peekachu passed away suddenly.”</p><p>The aquarium is planning a post-mortem to try to better understand Peekachu’s “overall health before she passed and what might have led to her death.”</p><p>Peekachu was part of a group of four belugas that arrived Aug. 13, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/07/21/4-beluga-whales-arrive-at-shedd-aquarium" target="_blank" ><u>joining four other beluga rescues that arrived from Marineland Canada July 21</u></a>. In total, Shedd is expected to house 16 belugas, including the eight already living at the aquarium before the Marineland whales arrived.</p><p>The Marineland belugas, a group of 30, had been living at the park, which has for years faced criticism that its animals were living in unsanitary conditions. The park closed to the public in 2024 and Marineland officials, citing extreme financial difficulties, had threatened to euthanize the whales if permanent homes couldn’t be found. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/08/12/shedd-aquarium-to-receive-four-more-beluga-whales-from-marineland" >Shedd Aquarium to receive four more beluga whales from Marineland</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/07/22/belugas-chicago-shedd-aquarium-marineland-canada-rescue" >Rescued belugas have arrived in Chicago. The move is unprecedented — and controversial</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-history/2026/08/07/beluga-whale-shedd-aquarium-abbott-oceanarium" >When Shedd Aquarium’s first beluga whales came to Chicago</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Mayor's executive order targets companies helping with deportation campaign, bans companies committing abuses
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson signed a wide-ranging executive order Wednesday meant to prevent corporations that carry out corrupt or abusive practices, including inhumanely assisting in aggressive federal deportation campaigns, from doing business with the city.</p><p>Citing an "unprecedented level of corporate corruption” nationally, the three-pronged order: prohibits contracts or subcontracts with a company that has committed workplace discrimination, wage theft, or a defined “public integrity violation” in the past five years; requires a company to disclose its diversity demographics, as well as any contracts it has with any other body of government, such as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE); and creates a 12-member Ethical Procurement Standards Task Force.</p><p>“You think about workers' rights, you think about voting rights, you think about the rights of the LGBTQ+ community. All of us are incredibly vulnerable right now. I'm working to do something about it,” Johnson told WBEZ in an interview Tuesday.</p><p>A public integrity violation includes some actions already banned in city code, such as a conviction of bribery. But unlike city code, it would apply to violations adjudicated outside a courtroom. For instance, a finding by a government oversight agency, like an inspector general or auditor, would also be disqualifying.</p><p>Johnson’s team cited Palantir, a data company profiting from contracts with ICE and the war in Gaza, as being among the corporations footing the bill for President Donald Trump’s ballroom under construction at the White House.</p><p>“We're recognizing that these companies may be engaging in corrupt activities, but for a variety of reasons may not be subject to criminal penalties. Nonetheless, we don't want them doing business with the city of Chicago,” said Johnson’s chief strategy officer, Sheila Bedi.</p><p>All current and future contractors and subcontractors will be required to certify that they have not committed a “public integrity violation” in the past five years, and don’t intend to for the length of a contract. The order directs the city’s chief procurement officer to come up with consequences for violating the new rules.</p><p>City code already bans contractors and subcontractors with any conviction involving theft, deceit, hate crimes, perjury, or treason. Those broader crimes don’t appear to be subject to the executive order, meaning they would still require a formal conviction to be disqualifying.</p><p>In response to Trump administration actions, the decree also contains new reporting requirements. Companies will have to disclose whether they hold contracts with other government or law enforcement agencies, which will then be made public. The order was prompted in part by a campaign called “Not With Our Money” that is pushing governments to use their purchasing power to dissuade companies from aiding or being complicit in militarized deportation campaigns.</p><p>“This is a way to say we want to look closely at what you're doing, and if you're doing corrupt things, then we're not going to use taxpayer dollars to support that,” said Dorian Warren, a spokesperson for Not With Our Money.</p><p>The campaign is currently in talks with New York City, Newark, New Jersey and Minneapolis but “Chicago is the first city to take action,” he said.</p><p>According to the campaign’s research team, Chicago currently holds $3.19 billion in contracts with companies that also do business with ICE. The biggest contract is with the infrastructure consultant AECOM, which is overseeing the modernization of O’Hare Airport, according to the group.</p><p>But Bedi said the goal isn’t to nix companies for simply holding a contract with ICE.</p><p>It also requires a company to disclose whether it has been involved in any allegations of excessive force, unlawful detention, unconstitutional policing or discrimination in relation to their government contract, which could then trigger action.</p><p>Johnson and Bedi said the executive order would not apply to the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/25/chicago-parking-meters-deal-stonepeak-ownership-transfer-city-council" > private equity firm Stonepeak </a>that is seeking to take over Chicago’s parking meters from the private company that currently owns them, because the parking meters are “an asset that we completely sold” and have no ownership interest in, Bedi said.</p><p>Stonepeak owns Omni International, an airline company criticized for carrying out deportation flights where detainees were allegedly shackled and denied food and water for more than 10 hours.</p><p>In response to recent news that the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission could stop requiring the collection of demographic data, the order also directs companies making more than $1 billion a year to disclose the composition of their corporate leadership, board of directors and their policies for promoting diversity.</p><p>The state already has a similar requirement for all publicly traded companies headquartered in Illinois with or without state contracts. The executive order would apply to large private companies seeking city business. All companies will also be required to report any efforts to recruit, hire, or promote formerly incarcerated people.</p><p>This is the sixth decree signed by Johnson this year, and the 26th of his term, as he turns to his executive power pen to avoid divisive political battles with a City Council majority that has grown increasingly distrusting of Johnson and his legislative efforts.</p><p>And it comes as Johnson prepares to announce whether he’ll run for reelection in a crowded field eager to unseat him.</p><p>“We certainly cannot rely upon a body of government when you have some members who are more interested in protecting the status quo in the interests of corporations,” Johnson said. “I have to do whatever is necessary.”</p>
