entries.title: Thornton's customer fatally shot moments after warning clerk of masked armed robbers
entries.summary: <p>A watchful Thornton's customer was fatally shot by masked armed robbers moments after warning the clerk when he spotted them outside the station early Tuesday in the Brighton Park neighborhood on the city's Southwest Side. </p><p>The attack unfolded <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/25/armed-robbers-fatally-shoot-man-36-during-heist-at-brighton-park-gas-station" target="_blank" >just before 3 a.m. Tuesday</a> when a white Hyundai with four men inside it pulled into the parking lot, and "circled" the station, at 3450 S. California Ave., according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times. </p><p>As one of the assailants got out and asked the clerk if he could use the washroom, the 36-year-old Willowbrook man, who had just parked next to them, entered the station to buy coffee and gas and he alerted the clerk there were "guys with masks in the lot," according to the report and sources. </p><p>The clerk told the 36-year-old man she'd lock the door after he left but as he was trying to leave, the other three assailants jumped out of the car and shot the man in the head, neck and chest before robbing the station of cash from one of the drawers, the report said. </p><p>The victim, who may have returned fire, was dead on the scene, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office and police. </p><p>Before the four robbers got back into the car and fled they took something that was lying next to the 36-year-old man, who had an empty holster, according to the report. His name hasn’t been released yet. </p><p>Ten nine-millimeter casings were found in two locations at the scene and suspected blood was also present, according to the police report. </p><p>Area 1 detectives continue to investigate. <br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Meta to pay Illinois up to $768 million as part of multistate settlement over teen social media addiction
entries.summary: <p>Meta has agreed to pay $17 billion and add child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction and settle claims filed by 47 states, state attorneys general announced Wednesday.</p><p>Illinios, California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were among 28 states that sued the tech giant in 2023, but the deal cuts short the trial, which was expected to see CEO Mark Zuckerberg take the stand before a jury in federal court in California.</p><p>It's one of the largest state consumer protection settlements in history, and Illinois will receive up to nearly $768 million under the settlement, according to the office of Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul.</p><p>“This is a monumental victory for online safety that will affect an entire generation of young people. After decades of putting profits before the health and wellness of children, this landmark settlement requires Meta to put our children’s safety and mental health at the forefront,” Raoul said in a news release.</p><p>Meta said in a blog post that it was “building on our longstanding efforts to empower parents and support teens.”</p><p>“Ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative for Meta,” the company said. “We want to get this right for parents and teens, and that’s why we partnered with state attorneys general to set a new industry standard."</p><p>The company urged its rivals to adopt similar safety measures.</p><p>The $17 billion settlement is a fraction of the company's 2025 revenue of $201 billion.</p><p>The lawsuit accused Meta of contributing to the youth mental health crisis by deliberately designing features that addict children to its platforms and hiding them from the public. It also argued that Meta violated federal laws by routinely collecting data on children under 13 without their parents’ consent.</p><p>The trial kicked off last week in Oakland, California, with U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers overseeing the proceedings. Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, began his testimony late Tuesday and defended Meta’s record and progress on child safety and privacy.</p><p>The cases in other states had been expected to go to trial later. In addition, nine attorneys general filed lawsuits in their respective states.</p><p>Under the proposed settlement, Meta agreed to adopt a series of safety features, including a “hard cap” on daily time limits and pauses for children using Instagram and Facebook.</p><p>It will eliminate push notifications during weekday school hours and bring in “robust” age-assurance measures and “age-appropriate” content controls to prevent bullying and harmful material about eating disorders and self-harm.</p><p>There will be stronger and more user-friendly parental controls and limits on social comparison features such as “like” counts.</p><p>The federal lawsuit was the result of an investigation led by a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general from California, Florida, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Nebraska, New Jersey, Tennessee, and Vermont. It followed newspaper reports, first by The Wall Street Journal in 2021, that found that the company knew about the harm Instagram can cause teenagers — especially teen girls — when it comes to mental health and body image issues.</p><p>Meta has since added a host of safety features to Instagram, including separate accounts for teenagers with stronger protections around messaging and privacy, along with content restrictions.</p><p>But child safety experts, along with some former Meta employees, have long contended that the features are little more than window dressing.</p><p>Arturo Béjar, a former Meta engineering director, said during his testimony last week that Meta consistently prioritized profits over safety in designing its products, focusing on how often and for how long people used them, even if it was detrimental to their mental well-being.</p><p>“If you step away from the product, they are not going to make any money,” he said.</p><p>While the four states in the Oakland trial did not officially say how much they had been seeking, Meta said in a court filing that financial penalties in the case could amount to as much as $1.4 trillion — a figure legal experts said was unlikely, if not impossible.</p><p><i>Contributing: Sun-Times staff</i></p>
entries.author: Kelvin Chan

entries.title: 3 men shot in Near West Side drive-by
entries.summary: <p>Three men are recovering at Stroger Hospital after being shot during a drive-by Tuesday night on the Near West Side. </p><p>The men were outside in the 2100 block of West Jackson Boulevard around 10:15 p.m. when a vehicle passed by and someone inside opened fire, Chicago police said. </p><p>Two men, 37 and 47, were shot in the left leg and were taken to Stroger Hospital where they were in good condition, police said. </p><p>The third man, 39, was shot in the abdomen and right leg and was also taken to Stroger where he was in fair condition, officials said. </p><p>No arrests have been made. </p><p>Area 3 detectives were investigating. </p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydbnhl-l-tk/" target="_blank" >Kyle MacMillan</a></h5><p>Singer-songwriter Natalie Merchant has spent years as an international star — first with the band 10,000 Maniacs and then as a solo artist. But one of her biggest musical satisfactions has nothing to do with the big-stage limelight.</p><p>Merchant’s "Cabinet of Wonder," a digital children's album, marks the culmination of an ongoing project she calls her "legacy." It's an ambitious educational collaboration with the Chicago Children's Theatre and Chicago Symphony Orchestra that features an accompanying website with recordings, videos and teaching aids free for teachers, parents, children and anyone else.</p><p>The concept behind it all is simple. Merchant has set 14 Mother Goose nursery rhymes to music, using the familiarity and metrical patterns of the venerable texts combined with her catchy tunes to teach preschool and kindergarten-age children a love for both music and language.</p><p>"Children deserve beauty," Merchant said, "and people who develop a sense of aesthetics at a really young age and who create beauty, make better citizens, make a better society, make a better world."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydbnhl-l-tu/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What's the most memorable meal you've had at a Chicago restaurant? entries.title: Chicago program that set aside billions for development has left poor areas behind, UIC study finds
entries.summary: <p>A program that has successfully helped revive Chicago’s once-downtrodden downtown has been less effective in the city’s poorer neighborhoods, including many on the South Side and West Side, <a class="Link" href="https://greatcities.uic.edu/news-stories/chicagos-tax-increment-financing-who-paid-who-gained/" target="_blank" ><u>a</u> <u>sweeping study published Wednesday found</u></a>.</p><p>Authorized by state lawmakers more than 40 years ago, tax-increment financing — known for short as TIF — aims to revitalize struggling neighborhoods by stimulating economic development. When the city designates a TIF district, it freezes the assessed property values in that area for at least 23 years. Any future extra tax revenue resulting from rising property values there is earmarked in a TIF fund and reinvested in the development of that same or surrounding area.</p><p>The money can be used for the construction of parks, schools and infrastructure, as well as for incentives for private commercial and residential development. As the theory goes, projects funded by TIF cause the value of the surrounding properties to rise, fueling more growth.</p><p>But the new study argues that nearly all of the increases in property values would have occurred without the program.</p><p>“Chicago has utilized this program far more than any other major American city,” said Juan González, a senior research fellow with the Great Cities Institute, an economic research hub at the University of Illinois Chicago that published the study. “Over the decades, the program morphed into a runaway development tool with little accountability to the public<i>.”</i></p><p>The researchers spent more than a year analyzing Chicago’s use of TIF since the program was first implemented downtown in 1984, reviewing contracts and creating a dataset that included property assessments and tax rates. The analysis relied on publicly available data, which spanned different periods and contained errors and gaps.</p><p>The program has thrived as intended downtown, now brimming with offices and restaurants. But the researchers found that it has been less successful in poorer areas, which have largely failed to see transformative change, partly because of decades of underinvestment.</p><p>Among the funds the researchers were able to track was $9.4 billion allocated for a mix of 1,427 public and private development projects across the city. Of nearly $2.6 billion in TIF funds used on private projects, 64% — around $1.6 billion — was allocated to five neighborhoods in and around downtown.</p><p>The researchers estimated that five communities on the South Sie and West Side received $55 million in TIF funds for private projects, barely half as much as the Near North Side, the lowest recipient among the downtown neighborhoods.</p><p>Downtown communities didn’t only benefit from private development. The researchers also found that almost half of TIF spending they tracked since 1986 for projects such as affordable housing, parks and roads also was concentrated in and around downtown.</p><p><i>“</i>Instead of reducing the city’s historic economic inequities, it has exacerbated<i> </i>them,” González said.</p><p>Jan Brueckner, a University of California, Irvine, economics professor who developed a model on TIF’s effects on public services in Illinois two decades ago, said the research was “well done.” Brueckner, who wasn't involved with the study, said TIF districts “collect tax revenue generated by improvements, as intended, but also keep revenue from overall property-value inflation, which is then not available to the city.”</p><p>Supporters of TIF have long argued that the program generates private investment, jobs and increased property value that would not have otherwise occurred.</p><p>But the researchers compared the change in value for properties that were closest to TIF projects to values for properties that were farther away. They found little difference, estimating that over 98% of the increase in property value within TIF districts would have happened without the program.</p><p>William Fulton, an urban studies professor at the University of California, San Diego, and a former San Diego city planner, who was not involved with the study, cautioned that the comparison was not an “apples to apples” and that the 98% figure was likely inflated.</p><p>“What it assumed is that the parcels in or near the TIF and the neighborhoods in or near the TIF are exactly the same as the parcels in the neighborhood a little further away, which may or may not be true,” Fulton said.</p><p>Critics argue that TIF diverts tax revenue that otherwise could have gone to local agencies, such as public school systems, fire and police departments and park districts, which have to divide up the amount of property tax frozen before a TIF area is designated.</p><p>The researchers concluded that homeowners faced higher property tax rates over time to make up for the diverted revenue. They assumed that, if the city had access to that revenue and applied the funds for basic services, property tax rates would not have increased as much. They estimated that a Chicago homeowner with a $300,000 home paid $878 in 2023 to make up for the amount of property tax revenue diverted to TIF. Overall, the researchers estimated the homeowner paid $6,616 from 2014 to 2023.</p><p>To calculate how much revenue was diverted to TIF and its possible effect on local agencies, the researchers analyzed tax bills from some of downtown’s most valuable properties.</p><p>Google’s Midwest headquarters, for example, paid $7.6 million in property taxes in 2025, of which 98.2% was funneled into a TIF account. The rest of the tax revenue was divided and distributed among city services.</p><p>The share of tax revenue that the Chicago Public Schools received in 2025 was $73,126, equivalent to roughly one teacher’s salary.</p><p>The researchers did not recommend eliminating the program. But they suggested reforms including implementing independent oversight and reducing the amount of property tax revenue diverted from basic city services.</p><p>They also suggested that the city phase out downtown TIF districts that have accomplished their goals, so local agencies could collect more tax revenue.</p><p>“There is no question that TIF is a powerful but flawed and inequitable tool for economic development,” said Griffin Krueger, a spokesman for Mayor Brandon Johnson.</p><p>The Johnson administration says it is moving away from relying on the program to spur development.Krueger pointed to a $1.25 billion housing and economic development bond that he said would be a “long-term source of flexible, equitable funding.”</p><p>When a TIF district expires, the tax revenue it holds goes back to local agencies. A portion of that revenue will help to fund the bond, which was approved in 2024.</p><p>The bond program aims to invest up to $3 billion across Chicago by 2028. The city says the program will prioritize affordable housing and commercial projects on the South Side and West Side.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/by/nell-salzman" target="_blank" ><i><u>Nell Salzman</u></i></a><i> reported this story as part of The New York Times’s</i><a class="Link" href="https://www.nytco.com/careers/local-investigations-fellowship/" target="_blank" ><i> <u>Local Investigations Fellowship</u></i></a><i>.</i></p>

entries.title: Bears training-camp report No. 19: Luther Burden, Darnell Wright return
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ Wednesday training camp practice:</p><h3>Burden back</h3><p>Bears receiver Luther Burden returned to practice after hurting his groin earlier Aug. 8 when he got tangled up with cornerback Tyrique Stevenson. The former second-round pick stretched with his teammates did individual drills for the first part of the hourlong practice.</p><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson and general manager Ryan Poles have both singled out Burden as a player they believe is bound for a breakthrough season. The Bears believed Burden would be back in plenty of time for their opener, which is two weeks from Sunday, and it looks like they were correct.</p><h3>Wright too</h3><p>That wasn’t the only piece of good news for the Bears. Right tackle <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/25/bears-rt-darnell-wright-leaves-practice-with-apparent-arm-injury" target="_blank" >Darnell Wright</a> left practice Tuesday after trainers examined the same right elbow he hurt last season — and for which he still wears a brace. He returned to practice Wednesday.</p><p>Defensive tackle Gervon Dexter, who left practice early Tuesday, did not practice. Dexter, who was running with the second team Tuesday before he left practice, is entering the final year of his contract. Defensive end Austin Booker remained out.</p><p>Safety Elijah Hicks and linebacker Keyshaun Elliott, who were activated off the physically-unable-to-perform list Tuesday, practiced for the first time Wednesday. Defensive tackle Grady Jarrett and guard Joe Thuney each got veteran off days.</p><h3>What’s next?</h3><p>After traveling to Nashville on Wednesday, the Bears will participate in a joint practice against the Titans at 11 a.m.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Man's body pulled from Belmont Harbor
entries.summary: <p>The body of a 22-year-old man was pulled from Lake Michigan Wednesday morning outside the Chicago Yacht Club in Belmont Harbor, police said. </p><p>After being recovered from the water, the 22-year-old was pronounced dead on the scene about 10:20 a.m. in the 300 block of West Belmont Avenue, police said. </p><p>It was not clear if foul play was involved. </p><p>Area 3 detectives are conducting a death investigation. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man, 26, critically wounded in Garfield Park shooting
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for a vehicle involved in a Wednesday morning shooting that left a 26-year-old man critically wounded.</p><p>About 10:15 a.m., a 26-year-old man was standing in the 3600 block of West Fifth Avenue when an assailant jumped from a vehicle and opened fire, police said. </p><p>He was hit in the head and taken to Mount Sinai Hospital in critical condition, police said. </p><p>The assailant, who fled in an unknown direction in the vehicle, was not arrested. </p><p>Area 4 detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Tim Curry, iconic character actor and 'Rocky Horror Picture Show' star, dies at 80
entries.summary: <p>Tim Curry, a character actor who created a gallery of delicious, very loony villains for stage and screen, including Dr. Frank-N-Furter in <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/television-general-news-b7f155629af749da93cec871b1728ab5" target="_blank" >“The Rocky Horror Picture Show,”</a> has died. He was 80.</p><p>Curry, who <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/video/tim-curry-shares-details-about-his-health-a75d87c9abf14caabed76243f6ed0ca4" target="_blank" >suffered a stroke in 2012</a> that put him in a wheelchair, died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles, according to his longtime manager and friend Marcia Hurwitz. No cause was disclosed.</p><p>Known for his arch humor, a putty-like face and gift with voices, Curry earned three Tony nominations — for “Spamalot,” “My Favorite Year” and “Amadeus” — and an Emmy nod in 1994.</p><p>“I like playing the more curious corners of the human mind and human behavior, partly because they’re a tad more interesting,” Curry told The Associated Press in 1993.</p><p>Curry burst onto the scene as the Transylvanian Frank-N-Furter in the sci-fi, cross-dressing rock musical “The Rocky Horror Picture Show,” which premiered in 1973 at the Royal Court Theatre in London. He went with it to Broadway and then starred in the 1975 cult-classic movie alongside Barry Bostwick, <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/meat-loaf-dead-b5cec094291a4e8a6f5f0f88aba18b4d" target="_blank" >Meat Loaf</a> and Susan Sarandon.</p><p>The show was ahead of its time in terms of its representation of LGBTQ+ characters and has entered the pop culture lexicon for its many iconic and memorable scenes, including the song “The Time Warp,” which has been covered by handfuls of artists, and the often-quoted phrase, “Dammit, Janet!” The show was twice revived on Broadway, most recently in 2026 with <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/tony-award-nomination-2026-572dbe6ce651561b6a6706a778b9708a" target="_blank" >Luke Evans playing Frank-N-Furter.</a></p><div data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Tim Curry performs a number from the musical “Spamalot” during the Broadway premiere on March 17, 2005, in New York.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Stuart Ramson/AP Photo/Stuart Ramson</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h4>Tim Curry’s take on Frank-N-Furter</h4><p>Curry's Frank-N-Furter had a posh British accent, but that almost wasn’t the case. He said he tried German and American accents but pivoted after he heard a British woman on a bus talking with her friend.</p><p>“I met a woman on a bus who said, ‘Do you have a house in town or a house in the country’ and I thought, ‘That’s the voice!’” he told LA Magazine in 2015.</p><p>For many years after the film’s premiere, the British-born actor declined to discuss it. He didn’t participate in activities promoting the film, which morphed into an interactive event at midnight shows. But he later warmed again to the project and embraced it at public events. Asked by LA Magazine how he viewed “Rocky Horror,” he responded: “With a sort of bemused tolerance. It’s neither a blessing nor a curse. I was lucky to get it.”</p><p>Curry’s Broadway career included starring in <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/stoppard-obit-britain-playwright-2721a8178c7e9691fdbd84e8fc9c0736" target="_blank" >Tom Stoppard’s “Travesties”</a> in 1975-76, playing Mozart opposite Ian McKellen’s Antonio Salieri in Peter Shaffer’s “Amadeus” and King Arthur in the 2005 production of “Spamalot.” The New York Times said his “stalwart, plummy-voiced Arthur wears a smile as inflexible as armor.”</p><p>His screen credits included starring as the child-killing monster in the 1990 miniseries version of Stephen King’s horror novel “It” and the double-dealing Cardinal Richelieu in 1993’s “The Three Musketeers” with Kiefer Sutherland, Charlie Sheen and Chris O’Donnell.</p><p>In his 2025 memoir, “Vagabond,” Curry warned readers that while there were scraps of his nature in his characters, he was none of them. “The distinctions between who I really am and who I've pretended to be as an actor have proven to be a source of great disappointment to some audiences. It has not caused me much personal distress beyond the periodic necessity to deter stalkers,” he wrote.</p><h4>Tim Curry’s life and career began in England</h4><p>Born in Cheshire, England, Curry was the son of a Navy chaplain and a school secretary. He was 12 when his father died and his mother subsequently went to work. Young Tim learned to cook his own breakfast, resulting in a lifelong passion for cooking, and sharpened his humor muscles.</p><p>“My father was a Methodist chaplain in the Navy, and we moved pretty much every 18 months,” he said. “So I had to make my mark in new schools and new playgrounds pretty quickly. And a sense of humor is the best way to do that. I was always a kind of mimic, one of those awful, relentless children, I should think.”</p><p>Acting did not occur to him until his middle teens, when he attended a school for the sons of Methodist ministers.</p><p>“I was lucky that it was a liberal kind of school; many of them in England are rather Dickensian,” he recalled to the AP. “There was a lot of theater, and I sang, too; I had been singing in church from the age of 7. I had enormous opportunities to express myself in that way. I just got hooked, really.”</p><p>His training continued in 1965 when he entered the University of Birmingham, at that time one of three English universities with a drama department. “I took an academic course, which I largely ignored, I’m afraid, and just acted all the time,” he said.</p><p>He then went down to London and talked his way into his first job, “Hair,” in the West End. Curry went on to the more formalized theater of the Royal Shakespeare Company and the Royal Court Theatre, where he was enlisted for “The Rocky Horror Picture Show.”</p><h4>Tim Curry’s other roles</h4><p>He went on, as the smug concierge, to futilely try to stop Macaulay Culkin's Kevin McCallister from taking advantage of New York’s swanky Plaza Hotel in “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York.” Curry also was Wadsworth, the unhinged butler with a secret past, in the also quotable “Clue.” He also played a wealthy philanthropist in 1995's “Congo” and opposite Carol Burnett in the movie “Annie.”</p><p>“Hollywood tends to use European actors, especially English ones, as villains because they prefer heroes to be Americans. I think we come with a certain amount of style, which is hard for American actors to acquire,” he told the AP in 1997. “They have to choose early on between New York and the theater vs. Hollywood and television and movies. In England there is still regional theater, where you can be assured work for several years doing all kinds of things.”</p><p>In later years, Curry lent his baritone voice to many voice-acting roles in children’s TV series, including “Star Wars: The Clone Wars,” “The Wild Thornberrys” and “The Adventures of Jimmy Neutron, Boy Genius.”</p><p>After a yearslong break from live-action roles, he played a plague doctor-masked man in a wheelchair in 2024's “Stream,” something the film's director Michael Leavy called a dream come true.</p><p>Curry, who never married and had no children, was deeply private about his personal life. But he wrote in his memoir that he was convinced to tell his story thanks to so many moving encounters with fans.</p><p>“The notion that my experiences might resonate helps me persevere — if they strike a chord with only one teenager, alone with a book in his room, as I so often was; or that young woman reading this on an interminably long bus ride; or that older queen, hopefully still in his fishnets, who saw ‘Rocky Horror’ upstairs at the Royal Court; or that middle-aged mother who organizes ‘Clue’ watching parties and refuses entry to anybody out of costume; or that buttoned-up bank clerk who relishes musicals; or that woman who kicked me out of the Waverly for being myself,” he wrote.</p>

entries.title: FDA approves landmark pancreatic cancer drug that's shown to improve survival
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON (AP) — The Food and Drug Administration on Wednesday approved a groundbreaking new drug for the most common form of pancreatic cancer, offering U.S. patients a more effective treatment against one of the deadliest <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/cancer" target="_blank" >types of cancer</a>.</p><p>FDA officials gave expedited approval to <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/pancreatic-cancer-daraxonrasib-chemotherapy-kras-62537cbc43c5286edb4c00806dc1c2de" target="_blank" >the first-of-a-kind pill</a>, called daraxonrasib, that blocks a mutated protein that fuels tumor growth in more than 90% of pancreatic cancer cases. It's an approach that previously eluded drugmakers for decades.</p><p>The daily pills will be sold by Revolution Medicines under the brand name Rasonque.</p><p>Patients taking the drug nearly doubled their survival time, with fewer severe side effects, in a study that randomly assigned them to receive the experimental treatment or more chemotherapy. The company-funded study enrolled 500 patients whose metastatic, or spreading, cancer had quit responding to prior treatment.</p><p>Patients getting the new treatment lived for a median of 13.2 months compared with 6.7 months for chemotherapy recipients.</p><p>Pancreatic cancer is among the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/cancer-survival-covid19-pandemic-delays-604acf08584f99c4f079d615ed8af501" target="_blank" >most deadly forms</a> in large part because it is hard to detect before it starts spreading to other organs. The American Cancer Society estimates about 67,000 new cases will be diagnosed in the United States this year and more than 52,000 people will die from the disease. The five-year overall survival rate is 13%.</p><p>The drug garnered public attention earlier this year when <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/ben-sasse-senator-pancreatic-cancer-40621aba0181385c950c0958e6231ddc" target="_blank" >former Sen. Ben Sasse</a>, R-Neb., described on CBS' “60 Minutes” how he has had less pain while taking it. A surge in public interest led the FDA to allow “expanded access,” before the drug’s official approval, for patients who met certain criteria.</p><p>FDA regulators noted on Wednesday that they approved the drug more than six months ahead of their target date.</p><p>"It is our fundamental duty to deliver more cures and meaningful treatments to patients as quickly as possible,” the FDA's acting commissioner, Kyle Diamantas, said in a statement.</p><p>Doctors who treat pancreatic cancer have expressed optimism that approval of the drug may usher in more new options, with dozens of experimental drugs in development. Unlike with other cancers that have benefited from a variety of chemotherapy alternatives, pancreatic cancer has been harder to tackle.</p><p>The new drug targets mutations in the RAS gene family that normally regulates cell growth. What are known as KRAS mutations are especially critical in fueling pancreatic cancer. But a structure that made it hard for drugs to stick to the mutated proteins meant this cancer driver was long considered “undruggable.”</p><p>Revolution Medicines’ drug uses what’s essentially a molecular glue to bind with multiple KRAS subtypes. The Redwood City, California-based drugmaker is studying its technology other forms of cancer, including lung cancer.</p><p>___</p><p>The Associated Press Health and Science Department receives support from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute’s Department of Science Education and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. The AP is solely responsible for all content.</p>

entries.title: Third suspect charged in 2024 slaying of mail carrier Octavia Redmond in West Pullman
entries.summary: <p>A third suspect — the apparent mastermind — has been charged in the attack of an on duty mail carrier Octavia Redmond who was gunned down in July 2024 as she delivered letters in a Far South Side neighborhood, Chicago police said.</p><p>Lyndell DeYoung, 35, was charged with murder, according to police. DeYoung, of the 7900 block of South Mozart Street, is due in court later Wednesday on the allegations.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/10/01/boy-15-charged-with-fatally-shooting-postal-worker-octavia-redmond-west-pullman" target="_blank" >Redmond had just delivered mail</a> to a home in the 12100 block of South Harvard Avenue when she was gunned down on July 19, 2024.</p><p>During his Monday arrest, DeYoung offered detectives a statement “outlining in full detail the motive and execution of the murder,” according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times.</p><p>In 2024, a 15-year-old was cited in a juvenile petition with murder and was the alleged triggerman and Yanheim C. Edwards — who allegedly drove the getaway car and then burned it, was charged with arson, according to the report.</p>

entries.title: Pritzker signs e-bike regulation bill into law
entries.summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker has signed legislation regulating e-bikes and other powered micromobility devices that have fueled a rise in emergency room visits among children.</p><p>The law codifies e-bikes to their current three-tiered classification, capped at 28 mph, and, starting Jan. 1, places new restrictions for most devices capable of going any faster.</p><p>The law classifies any device capable of going faster than 28 mph as motor vehicles and subjects their operators to the state’s drunken driving laws, according to the legislation <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/06/04/e-bike-moto-regulation-illinois-pritzker-giannoulias" target="_blank" >passed by lawmakers in June</a>.</p><p>Owners of those high-speed devices — which can include e-bikes, e-motos, e-scooters, electric unicycles, electric skateboards — will be required to have a driver’s license, carry insurance and register their vehicle with the state. They will not be allowed on bike paths and, in some cases, bike lanes.</p><p>The law creates consistent rules for the devices across the state, eliminating a growing and inconsistent patchwork of local ordinances.</p><p>The law also introduces age minimums for e-bikes and e-scooters, seeking to address a rise in injuries among children using the devices. One study found a 7.5-fold <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/graphics/2026/07/29/e-bike-injuries-child-kids-safety-health-transit/90956259007/" target="_blank" >increase</a> in children on the devices seeking emergency care from 2023 to 2026.</p><p>Riders of Class 1 and Class 2 e-bikes, which go up to 20 mph, must be at least 15 years old, according to the law. Riders must be at least 16 years old for Class 3 e-bikes, which go up to 28 mph. E-scooter users must be at least 16 years old, and are capped at 15 mph.</p><p>Pritzker's team said he signed the bill into law on Wednesday but did not have any immediate comment.</p><p>State Sen. Darby Hills, a Republican from Barrington Hills, praised the bill's signing for its age restrictions.</p><p>"As a mom, there is nothing more important to me than making sure our kids can get outside, have fun, and get home safely," Hills said in a statement. "That’s why I’m so proud to see our e-bike safety legislation signed into law."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Seven under-the-radar quarterbacks who opened eyes in Week 1
entries.summary: <p>Much of the preseason was focused on the area’s star quarterbacks. Montini’s Israel Abrams and Jake Nawrot of Hersey are ranked in the top five in the nation by 247Sports.com, and there are four more Power Four committed quarterbacks in the area: Batavia’s Michael Vander Luitgaren (Wyoming), Maine South’s Jameson Purcell (Indiana) and Jackie Ryder of New Trier (Purdue).</p><p>A new star emerged in Week 1. Brother Rice freshman Sam Holcomb, who is splitting time with senior Rocco Galasso at quarterback, wowed observers in the Crusaders’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/21/lincoln-way-east-football-brother-rice" >loss at Lincoln-Way East.</a></p><p>Holcomb, 6-1, already holds a scholarship offer from Michigan. He was 11 of 15 for 109 yards with one TD and no interceptions against the Griffins and was a major threat on the ground with six carries for 59 yards and 2 TDs.</p><p>It is rare for a freshman quarterback to start at any school, but especially in the highly competitive Catholic League Blue.</p><p>Jonas Williams, now at USC, started as a freshman at Bolingbrook. And Logan Malachuk took over the starting job for Nazareth as a freshman in 2021. But even Trae Taylor, now considered the top senior quarterback in the country, wasn’t a starter at Carmel his first year.</p><p>Holcomb’s debut wasn’t the only intriguing quarterback performance in Week 1. Here’s a look at six other notable performers on the opening weekend.</p><h3>Myles Hill, Fenwick</h3><p>Hill’s first pass in his first start was spectacular. The 6-0 junior connected with Jimmy Watts for an 84-yard TD. The defending Class 6A champs have a lot of new faces this season, but Hill’s quick start answered one question definitively. He completed 16 of 21 passes for 214 yards wand 3 TDs in the Friars’ win against Joliet Catholic.</p><h3>Jake Fleming, Marist</h3><p>The junior threw three touchdown passes <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-sports/2026/08/22/fleming-brothers-help-lift-marist-past-visiting-simeon" >against Simeon</a> in his varsity debut. Two of the scores went to his brother Conor, a sophomore also making his debut. Fleming was 12 of 17 for 259 yards.</p><h3>AJ Rogers, Wheaton-Warrenville South</h3><p>The standout baseball and basketball player made his presence felt on the football field in his first varsity start. Rogers, a 6-3 junior, was 16 of 23 passing for 201 yards and 2 TDs and had nine carries for 47 yards in the Tigers’ win against Naperville Central. Wheaton-Warrenville South coach Sean Norris believes Rogers is one of the best junior quarterbacks in the state.</p><h3>Marion Persich, Morris</h3><p>Persich’s transfer from LaSalle-Peru to Morris was one of the major moves of the offseason. The 6-4 junior fit right in with the Warriors in Week 1, accounting for five touchdowns in a win against Lemont. Persich was 8 of 10 passing for 111 yards and 2 TDs and rushed for 176 yards and 3 TDs.</p><h3>Gavin Gardiner, St. Patrick</h3><h3></h3><p>The Shamrocks’ win against Rolling Meadows in Week 1 wasn’t Gardiner’s debut, and he isn’t a new young player to watch. But the senior has grown from 6-2 to 6-6 and may be poised for a breakout season. Gardiner threw for more than 2,000 yards last season and opened this year with 274 total yards. He threw for 3 TDs and ran for a score.</p><h3>Nate Lang, IC Catholic</h3><p>The senior was underrated heading into the season after throwing for 2,431 yards and 28 TDs with just 4 interceptions last season. Lang helped engineer a Week 1 upset of highly-regarded Nazareth, completing 19 of 25 passes for 252 yards and 3 TDs.</p>

entries.title: Foxtrot plans new Lake View location
entries.summary: <p>Specialty grocer Foxtrot is set to open<b> </b>a new location in Lake View next year, the company said Wednesday.</p><p>The location takes over a former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/restaurants/2026/08/03/ann-sather-stellas-diner" >Ann Sather Restaurant</a> space and will be part of the new mixed-use residential building, called the Belmora, at 917 W. Belmont Ave.</p><p>“Foxtrot was created as a neighborhood gathering place, and Belmora’s walkable, transit-oriented location makes it a natural fit for our next Chicago store,” Foxtrot Chief Operating Officer Jason DaPisa said in a statement.</p><p>The five-story Belmora project by Chicago-based <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/15/loop-building-residential-wave-office-conversions" >Mavrek Development</a> will have 46 apartments. The first phase at 919 W. Belmont Ave. is expected to open in the fall. Pre-leasing is already underway by real estate firm Cross Street. The second phase, at 917 W. Belmont, will also have 46 apartments, Crain's reported. </p><p>Mavrek and Cross Street didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>In April 2024, Foxtrot's parent company Outfox Hospitality abruptly closed all of its locations then a month later <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2024/05/15/doms-kitchen-market-foxtrot-outfox-chapter7-bankruptcy" >filed Chapter 7 bankruptcy</a>. Foxtrot’s assets were sold in an online auction to New York investment firm Further Point Enterprises for $2.2 million in May 2024. Further Point brought in key players from the old company, including Foxtrot co-founder Mike LaVitola as chairman.</p><p>In the two years since its store closings, the upscale grocer has reopened nine Chicago locations, as well as two stores in Dallas.</p><p>Prior to closing, Foxtrot had a location in Lake View at North Clark Street and West Diversey Parkway. Now, the company is plotting its return to the neighborhood.</p><p>“We’re excited to rejoin the Lakeview community and provide residents and neighbors with a convenient home for any daypart that suits their needs, whether it be morning coffee and breakfast tacos, lunchtime sweets and a fresh panini, or a bottle of wine and that last grocery item to complete the dinner plans,” DaPisa said. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2024/09/20/foxtrot-new-owners-further-point-lavitola-rebuild-community-trust-abrupt-grocery-closures-stunned" >Foxtrot’s new owners look to rebuild community trust after abrupt closures left many stunned</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2024/09/05/foxtrot-gold-coast-reopens" >Foxtrot’s patrons, staff savor reopening of Gold Coast store: ‘It’s just “Ahh.”’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2024/04/23/doms-kitchen-foxtrot-closing-stores-grocers-outfox-hospitality-merged" >Dom’s Kitchen and Foxtrot abruptly shutter stores, months after specialty grocers merged</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Projecting the Bears' 53-man roster with cut day looming
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ Roschon Johnson knows how to be patient — at Texas, he played behind all-world running back Bijan Robinson. But he admits that he grew frustrated last season when, as a result of injury, ineffectiveness, he carried the ball exactly twice.</p><p>It's been refreshing, then, for the special teams contributor to be the Bears’ starting running back in each of their two preseason games, totaling 12 carries.</p><p>“I can be a back that you can plug in and be productive with …” he said. “I have my own skillset …. I think I’m a powerful runner … that gets those hidden yards.”</p><p>Coach Ben Johnson has singled out starting left tackle and free safety as the two position battles still up in the air. There are other jobs, like Roschon Johnson’s, that will be decided before the team has to cut its roster to 53 players Sunday.</p><p>Here’s where they stand:</p><h3>OFFENSE (25 keepers)</h3><p><b>Quarterback (3 out of 4 kept)</b></p><p><b>They’re on the team:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/01/bears-qb-caleb-williams-must-keep-climbing-no-matter-how-it-goes-with-offensive-line-this-season" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a>, Tyson Bagent, Case Keenum<br><b>Work to do:</b> Miller Moss<br><b>What’s left to answer:</b> Whether the Bears will carry Moss, a former Williams teammate at USC, on their practice squad.<br><b>Number to know:</b> 158.3 — Keenum’s passer rating in the preseason opener</p><p><b>Running back (4/5)</b></p><p><b>They’re on the team:</b> D’Andre Swift, Kyle Monangai, Roschon Johnson, Salvon Ahmed<br><b>Work to do:</b>  Brittan Brown<br><b>What’s left to answer: </b>Whether<b> </b>the Bears can justify keeping four running backs. It likely depends on whether they believe that Monangai’s knee will heal in time for Week 1. Ahmed has been thrilling with the ball in his hand, while Johnson is the better special teamer.<br><b>Number to know:</b>  0 — Snaps played this preseason by Swift, with whom the Bears have been thrilled.</p><p><b>Tight end (3/6)</b><br><b>They’re on the team:</b> Cole Kmet, Colston Loveland, Sam Roush<br><b>Work to do:</b> Stephen Carlson, Hayden Large, Qadir Ismail<br><b>What’s left to answer:</b> Whether the team decides to keep Carlson as a fourth tight end — or whether coach Ben Johnson decides instead to use backup tackle Theo Benedet as an extra blocker.<br><b>Number to know:</b> 3 — The Bears’ top three tight ends were drafted in Rounds 1, 2 and 3.</p><p><b>Wide receiver (6/11)</b><br><b>They’re on the team:</b>  Rome Odunze, Luther Burden, Kalif Raymond, Jahdae Walker, Zavion Thomas, Kaden Davis<br><b>Work to do:</b> Scotty Miller, JP Richardson, Maurice Alexander, Omari Kelly, Ray-Ray McCloud III,<br><b>What’s left to answer:</b>  Davis, who spent the spring toiling in the UFL, has been one of the stars of training camp, making a wow play almost every day. But can the Bears trust him on special teams?<br><b>Number to know:</b> 0 — Career regular-season NFL catches for Davis.</p><p><b>Offensive line (9/17)</b><br><b>They’re on the team:</b> Braxton Jones, Joe Thuney, Garrett Bradbury, Jonah Jackson, Darnell Wright, Theo Benedet, Logan Jones, Luke Newman, Ozzy Trapilo<br><b>Work to do:</b> Jedrick Wills, Kiran Amegadjie, Jordan McFadden, Mason Murphy, Jaren Kump, Caden Barnett, Kyle Hergel, Wesley French<br><b>What’s left to answer: </b>What will the Bears do with Amegadjie? He’s three years away from being a third-round pick, so teams figure to dig into their scouting notes if and when the Bears waive him.<br><b>Number to know:</b> 7 — Months after patellar tendon surgery that Trapilo was able to return to the practice field. When he got hurt in Round 1 of the playoffs, the Bears feared he’d miss the whole season. He needs a few more weeks of practice before he can play in games.</p><h3>DEFENSE (25/44)</h3><p><b>Defensive line (10/15)</b></p><p><b>They’re on the team:</b> Montez Sweat, Austin Booker, Gervon Dexter, Grady Jarrett, Neville Gallimore, Daniel Hardy, Dayo Odeyingbo, Kentavius Street, Jordan van den Berg. Marcus Davenport. Shemar Turner is likely to start the season on PUP or injured reserve.<br><b>Work to do:</b>  Jamree Kromah, Jayden Loving, James Lynch, Jeremiah Martin<br><b>What’s left to answer:</b> Does Dexter get traded? He’s started 33 games for the Bears in three years and has garnered some interest, given that his contract expires at the end of the season. The Bears need all the defensive line help they can get, though, even with van den Berg flashing throughout camp.<br><b>Number to know:</b> 0 — Full practices Davenport has participated in since signing Aug. 17.</p><p><b>Linebacker (5/10)</b><br><b>They’re on the team:</b> Devin Bush, TJ Edwards, D’Marco Jackson, Jack Sanborn, Ruben Hyppolite<br><b>Work to do:</b> Jon Rhattigan, Keyshaun Elliott, Tony Fields, Antonio Greer, Wayne Matthews<br><b>What’s left to answer: </b>Does Elliott have time to get up to speed on special teams after being activated from PUP on Tuesday?  <br><b>Number to know:</b> 125 — Tackles Bush had with the Browns last year, more than any Bear.</p><p><b>Cornerback (6/11)</b><br><b>They’re on the team:</b> Jaylon Johnson, Tyrique Stevenson, Jaylon Jones, Josh Blackwell, Malik Muhammad, Terell Smith. Kyler Gordon will likely open the season on PUP.<br><b>Work to do:</b> Beanie Bishop, Dontae Manning, Deantre Prince, William Wright<br><b>What’s left to answer:</b> Is Bishop worth the trouble? If he makes the team, he must serve a three-game NFL suspension issued him before he signed with the Bears.<br><b>Number to know:</b> 4 — Games Gordon would have to miss, at minimum, if the Bears put him on PUP to start the season.</p><p><b>Safety (4/8)</b><br><b>They’re on the team:</b> Dillon Thieneman, Elijah Hicks, Cam Lewis, Xavier Woods. Coby Bryant, who is out for most of the season, will be put on injured reserve after cuts are made.<br><b>Work to do:</b> Anthony Johnson Jr., Marlen Sewell, Skyler Thomas<br><b>What’s left to answer:</b> Is Lewis a better safety than slot cornerback? The signing of Woods and the return of Hicks from injury gives the Bears flexibility to move him around.<br><b>Number to know:</b> 134 — Career games played by Woods, whom the Bears signed after Bryant got hurt.</p><h3>SPECIAL TEAMS (3/3)</h3><p><b>He’s on the team:</b> K Cairo Santos, P Tory Taylor, LS Beau Gardner<br><b>What’s left to answer:</b> Whether the Bears find a veteran on cut they like better than Gardner.<br><b>Number to know:</b>  0 — Gardner’s career NFL snaps.<br></p>

entries.title: Cleared of sex abuse claim, Pfleger blasts 'unjust' archdiocese probe
entries.summary: <p>In his first public comments since being reinstated at St. Sabina Catholic Church following a decades-old, unfounded sex abuse claim, the Rev. Michael Pfleger stood flanked by dozens of supporters outside the church Wednesday with a promise to "turn the volume up" on everything from pressing social justice issues to how accusations against priests are investigated. </p><p>"This accusation and others will follow me to the end of my life; in my obituary, they'll be talking about these accusations," Pfleger said. "But what I do know is this: The God that holds me and the faith community of St. Sabina, who's known me for 51 years, they know Mike Pfleger." </p><p>In July, Pfleger was accused of sexually abusing a girl who was a student at St. Sabina between 1993 and 1995. It was the fifth similar accusation against Pfleger within five years. said. "The policy makes no room for the accused to be taken seriously or receive justice."</p><p>"I, nor any priest, should be thrown under the bus by the very archdiocese I have given 51 years of my life serving," Pfleger added. </p><p>In a previously released statement, Cardinal Blase Cupich said, "I want to recognize the suffering you and Father Mike have endured, for I know his absence has been real and painful. But I ask you to allow God’s Word this weekend to free you from any sadness and disappointment."</p><p>James Figliulo, Pfleger's attorney, called on the archdiocese and city officials to designate a day celebrating St. Sabina. </p><p>"[There is] no legacy of sexual abuse and unfair allegations, the legacy of St. Sabina's is moral courage ... to show respect when there's disrespect," Figliulo said. </p><p>Alba Gonzalez and Barbara Morgan, two devout supporters of Pfleger, said the community went through the hardships with Pfleger "together as a family."</p><p>"This is not the first time," said Morgan, a member of the church since 1991. "The truth always makes room for itself. No one ever has to defend the truth."</p><p>Supporters are calling on the archdiocese to publicly apologize to Pfleger over the investigation's process, which included Pfleger being removed from his position as priest at the church. </p><p>"They need to publicly apologize to [Pfleger] and to us for what they put us through," Gonzalez said.</p><p>While they couldn’t get into specific details about the accusation, Figliulo and Pfleger described it as "an open-and-shut case that should've taken two weeks but took six instead."</p><p>"This is not just about my accusation being proven false," Pfleger said. "I am not going to stop fighting until this process is changed.</p><p>"We can still protect children and provide a fair process for the priests."</p><p><i>Contributing: Mary Norkol</i> </p>

entries.title: K-pop band BTS world tour ‘Arirang' in Chicago unites fans
entries.summary: <p>It's been seven years since K-pop superstars BTS have been in Chicago. But the group’s fans have kept the fire burning during that time.</p><p>Earlier this month Gov. JB Pritzker declared Aug. 27 and 28 “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/arts-and-culture/2026/08/20/gov-jb-pritzker-declares-bts-day-in-illinois-in-honor-of-k-pop-groups-visit-bts-chicago-soldier-field" target="_blank" >BTS Day</a>” in Illinois as a result of petitioning by Chicago BTS Army and the HANA Center, an immigrant advocacy nonprofit in Irving Park. And ahead of BTS’ return to Chicago this week, fans have been gathering to bond over their shared love of the K-pop titans, including a trivia night at Lincoln Park’s Replay on Tuesday.</p><p>Between the arcade games in Replay, the tables and bar are packed with buzzing BTS fans ahead of the South Korean superstars’ sold-out “Arirang” world tour shows Aug. 27-28 at Soldier Field.</p><div At the podium calling out the results was Mollie Menuck, 25, manager at KPOP Merch by Choc Choc. It’s the third trivia event that the Lake View store has hosted.</p><p>Menuck said became a BTS fan in 2021 thanks to her friend, but she was always a boy band lover, citing groups like One Direction, 5SOS and Why Don't We.</p><p>“My really good friend at the time was shoving K-pop down my throat, and I started watching the music videos. entries.title: Ben Brown hits setback in quest to return to Cubs as bullpen arm for season’s home stretch and playoffs
entries.summary: <p>PHOENIX – Potentially nearing the end of a monthslong rehab from a stress fracture in a vertebra in his neck, right-hander Ben Brown is once again trapped in the unknown.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> right-hander experienced symptoms in his neck at the end of a two-inning, 34-pitch appearance in a “bridge league” game Tuesday in Arizona, with those symptoms worsening as the day went on.</p><p>It’s forcing the Cubs to “regroup,” according to manager Craig Counsell, who said Brown will return to Chicago with the team and check in with doctors.</p><p>“Not sure yet what this means,” Counsell said Wednesday, “but it’s going to slow it down in some way.”</p><p>Brown, who excelled with a 1.70 ERA in eight starts before hitting the injured list in late June, appeared on track to return at some point next month as a bullpen arm, an intriguing possibility for a Cubs team eyeing a lengthy playoff run.</p><p>But this setback, which occurred during what was basically an organized scrimmage at the Cubs’ spring-training complex, raises the question of what, if anything, he’ll be able to contribute for the team this season.</p><p>“He’s felt so good. We’ve had no bad news,” Counsell said. “This is the first day of bad news.”</p><p>Brown’s injury turned out to be the same one that cost him much of his 2024 campaign, though the Cubs didn’t know that at the time, with the 26-year-old revealing in June that the diagnosis of a benign growth on a bone in his neck, an osteoma, had been “totally wrong” two years ago.</p><p>Brown <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/27/cubs-ben-brown-neck-injury-recovery-timeline-starting-rotation-pitching-injuries-justin-steele-rotation" >viewed that clarity as a blessing in disguise</a> and hoped the knowledge would allow him to find a way to pitch that would prevent this from being a recurring problem throughout his career.</p><p>But regardless of any work toward that long-term goal that might have taken place while Brown was on the injured list the last two months, the reemergence of symptoms on the doorstep of a possible minor league rehab stint has thrown a wrench into plans to get him back on the mound and help the Cubs in their quest for a World Series title this season.</p><p>Brown is one of numerous starters who could be in the running for relief roles in the playoffs, alongside the likes of righties Edward Cabrera, Javier Assad, Colin Rea and Aaron Civale.</p><p>The Cubs will have to wait to find out whether Brown can remain in that group of possibilities or not.</p><p>In the longer-term future, Brown figures to be a contender for a spot in what could be a very different-looking Cubs rotation next season.</p><p>The entirety of the at-this-moment starting staff – righties Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes, plus lefties Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and David Peterson – <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/20/cade-townsend-is-cubs-pitchings-far-future-but-whats-near-future-look-like-when-starters-hit-free-agency" >could depart via free agency</a>.</p><p>But Brown and other contenders – Cabrera, fellow righty Cade Horton and lefty Justin Steele – will be returning from injuries of varying significance.</p>

entries.title: Lawmakers, advocates allege Chicago immigration court violated due process for minors handed removal orders
entries.summary: <p>U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin and local advocates sounded the alarm Wednesday over systemic due process violations at Chicago's downtown immigration court, calling a strategy to speed up their cases and issue deportation orders to unaccompanied minors a "mockery of the justice system."</p><p>Durbin, U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley, and state leaders spoke out after attending a morning hearing, where they and courtroom advocates witnessed six minors handed removal orders.</p><p>“These kids, some as young as 12 years old are now being deported from the United States," Durbin said. “It's happening right here in the city of Chicago in the Loop. This is not what America is all about."</p><p>Quigley, a former defense attorney, echoed the senator’s outrage.</p><p>"What I saw today—and I practiced criminal defense for 17 years right here in Cook County—was a mockery of the justice system," Quigley said.</p><p>Advocates say since June they’ve seen a surge in cases involving unaccompanied children being called to show up to immigration court. Many of these minors have a pending Special Immigrant Juvenile Status which is a unique legal pathway created by Congress to protect children without legal status who have survived severe trauma at home. Though the program faces huge backlogs.</p><p>This strategy is part of ongoing shifting policies by the Department of Justice’s Executive Office for Immigration Review. For months, the agency has been speeding up asylum cases, reshuffling and scheduling mass hearings and issuing far more removal orders.</p><p>In a written statement a DOJ spokesperson said: “The Biden Administration allowed millions of unvetted aliens into our communities and intentionally turned a blind eye to hundreds of thousands of unaccompanied alien children in need of care. Reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration.”</p><p>But immigration advocates argue that the Trump administration’s fast-tracked focus on backlog statistics ignores the due process these minors are entitled to under the law.</p><p>“There are children in the United States alone, with no family here caring for them,” said Laura Smith, executive director of the Children’s Legal Center, which represents children in immigration custody. “These children fled to the U.S. seeking protection from horrors no child should endure—children who have been kidnapped, whose parents have been killed, or who have been completely abandoned.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Laura Smith Executive of the Children’s Legal Center, joined other elected officials, legal service providers, and advocates to discuss, due process violations currently targeting unaccompanied immigrant children at the Chicago Immigration Court at a press conference at the National Immigrant Justice Center in downtown Chicago on Aug. 26, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The six children ordered removed Wednesday range in age from 12 to 17, despite their applications for Special Immigrant Juvenile Status still pending, according to legal advocates.</p><p>In July, two were ordered removed that had approved this special status.</p><p>Smith says this move by the government is new. She explains that typically minors who are in the process of applying for a special immigrant juvenile status are shielded from removal orders.</p><p>Smith and other advocates with the National Immigrant Justice Center say the federal government is forcing children to appear in court every two weeks instead of a few times a year. Many of these minors are currently held in federal custody by the Office of Refugee Resettlement, living in various government facilities and long-term foster care homes.</p><p>“When we have had special immigrant juvenile status, it has meant termination of removal proceedings, and that the child gets to apply for residency, Smith said. “And the reason it's been that way the entire time that it's existed is because that is the law.” </p><p>Advocates say they plan to appeal the fast-tracked removal orders to the Board of Immigration Appeals. A loss there would trigger a final deportation order. Smith says attorneys will then prepare an emergency appeal to the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to pause removals.</p><p>Blasting recent federal programs cuts to support unaccompanied minors, including legal aid, advocates and lawmakers say they want the Trump administration to enforce existing protections. They argue federal statutes explicitly guarantee children access to a lawyer, a fair hearing outside a high-stakes deportation track, and a clear path to release.</p><p>They are asking the federal government to abide by current laws already passed by Congress and the states. </p><p><i>Adriana Cardona-Maguigad covers immigration for WBEZ. Follow her on X </i><a class="Link" href="https://twitter.com/AdrianaCardMag" target="_blank" >@AdrianaCardMag</a>.</p>

entries.title: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs fume over umps missing balk: ‘They find new ways to screw something up every day’
entries.summary: <p>PHOENIX – For the second time in a week, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> were left fuming over balk-related drama in the aftermath of a tough defeat.</p><p>“They flat out missed it,” manager Craig Counsell said. “It’s obvious to everybody on TV. It’s obvious to anybody. They missed it.”</p><p>What was obvious – to even the umpires themselves after they took a look at the video after the game – was that Diamondbacks lefty Eduardo Rodriguez was flustered by center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong moving down the third-base line in the sixth inning of a scoreless game Wednesday.</p><p>Rodriguez moved his feet in the middle of his delivery, stepping off the rubber, and the Cubs believed they got a successful outcome of Crow-Armstrong’s antagonizing – and a run on the scoreboard.</p><p>Except the umpiring crew didn’t see it that way, not in the moment, at least. They gathered to discuss it, and there was no balk call.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong – whose double to get him on base that inning was his only hit in 12 at-bats in the series – was livid, reacting so emotionally toward the umpires that he needed to be held back by third-base coach Quintin Berry. Counsell came out to argue, somewhat demonstrably, as well. Neither was ejected.</p><p>But the Cubs didn’t get their run, with first baseman Michael Busch walking and second baseman Nico Hoerner striking out against Rodriguez – who held the Cubs to just two hits in seven innings – to end the inning.</p><p>Moments later, lefty starter Matthew Boyd surrendered a go-ahead home run, and the Cubs suffered a 2-0 loss that cost them the series and wrapped their road trip out West at 2-4.</p><p>“I saw four umpires miss a pretty obvious play,” Crow-Armstrong said after the game. “They’re out there every day, just like we are. Their one job is to get calls right, and if they get it wrong, they’re supposed to talk about it, figure it out and get it right. And they didn’t.</p><p>“When a guy is shoving it down your throat, you’ve got to find any way you can to make something happen, and that’s exactly what I was trying to do. I executed, and it would have been nice if the umpires did the same.</p><p>“You guys just saw my frustrations from the last three days come out, and I’m going to stick by it and say, ‘Rightfully so.’ … I think they find new ways to screw something up every day.”</p><p>There wasn’t much consolation to be had in the umpires admitting their mistake after the game.</p><p>“We just didn’t see it,” crew chief Alfonso Marquez told a pool reporter. “After looking at the video, it looked like [Rodriguez] stepped off.”</p><p>“It doesn’t make me feel any better that they admitted that they missed the call,” Crow-Armstrong said. “They had as much time as they wanted to talk about it on the field. They should have admitted that right after they got it wrong.”</p><p>Earlier on the road trip, Friday in Seattle, the Cubs were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/22/cubs-matthew-boyd-pickoff-balk-craig-counsell-ejected-umpire" >steaming over a balk they didn’t think should have been called</a> against Boyd on a pickoff move, with Counsell saying that night, “It’s a situation where the umpire got fooled and made up a call because he got fooled.”</p><p>They lost that game on a walk-off hit in extra innings, and that became a theme during their six-game trip: Three of their four losses came in walk-off fashion.</p><p>Wednesday was the lone defeat they didn’t take in the last at-bat, with the bats stymied by Rodriguez. Crow-Armstrong struck out three times after going hitless Monday and Tuesday, taking his frustrations out on helmets, gloves, bats and other equipment before his on-field outburst over the non-call.</p><p>A rough series in Arizona doesn’t take away from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/05/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-shohei-ohtani-nl-mvp-race-dodgers-playoffs-craig-counsell-shota-imanaga" >his MVP-caliber season</a>, and the Cubs have no interest in Crow-Armstrong toning down the emotion he’s made a trademark of his game.</p><p>“I’ll take the plane ride and my golf outing to evaluate,” Crow-Armstrong said, “but I’ll get over myself on the golf course tomorrow and we’ll keep it pushing.”</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Fever-Sky game averages 3.31M viewers, most-watched regular-season WNBA game since 1997
entries.summary: <p>The Indiana Fever-Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" >Sky</a> game Sunday averaged 3.31 million viewers on NBC and Peacock to make it the most-watched regular-season WNBA game since the league's inaugural season in 1997.</p><p>It also was the third-most watched regular-season game ever and peaked at 3.82 million viewers. That is behind only the June 21-22, 1997 opening weekend games that featured the New York Liberty-Los Angeles Sparks (5.04 million) and Charlotte Sting-Phoenix Mercury (3.59 million), also both on NBC.</p><p>Caitlin Clark and the Fever continue to be the league's top draw. They also have set all-time viewing records this season for games on CBS, ESPN and Amazon Prime Video.<br>Against the Sky, Clark made a career-high eight 3-pointers and scored 37 points in the Fever's 113-90 victory. Teammate Kelsey Mitchell added 30.</p><p>That game was the first meeting since Chicago's DiJonai Carrington fouled Indiana's Sophie Cunningham on a breakaway in the Fever’s 90-86 victory on Aug. 8. Carrington was ejected for the Flagrant 2 foul.</p><p>There were no such incidents between the two in the rematch.</p><p>But there was controversy. Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom attended as a spectator and was ejected in the third quarter after he and the Sky's Natasha Cloud exchanged words. Freedom has since been banned from Sky home games.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: West Englewood's shuttered Charles Warrington Earle School reopens as affordable housing
entries.summary: <p>The former Charles Warrington Earle School — one of 50 Chicago schools that shuttered in 2013 — is taking on a second life as an affordable apartment building, with roughly a third of its units already leased.</p><p>Project and city leaders cut the ribbon Wednesday on the Earle Residences at 1711 W. 61st St. in West Englewood. The project has been almost a decade in the making and is one of several school-to-residential conversions that Wisconsin-based Gorman & Co. is completing in Chicago.</p><p>The Earle's 50 apartments are about 34% leased, according to Matt Burbach, Gorman’s director of development for Illinois. </p><p>Units include one- and two-bedrooms and are available to households making 60% of the area median income, or AMI. For a Chicago couple, that’s a combined annual income of $58,320.</p><p>Nine units are supported by the nonprofit Chicago Low-Income Housing Trust Fund's MAUI program, making them available for households at 15% AMI. MAUI stands for Multiyear Affordability through Upfront Investment, and the program offers interest-free forgivable loans to replace up to 50% of a developer’s private first mortgage loan, according to the nonprofit.</p><p>“This is a working-class development. It is for our working-class neighbors,” Chicago Department of Housing Commissioner Lissette Castañeda said.</p><p>The Earle has a community room, computer lab, fitness room, playground, community garden, laundry facilities and green space — amenities that “are not luxuries ... [but] what we need to thrive,” Castañeda said.</p><p>Gorman is also partnering with Chicago-based Phoenix Foundation and Phoenix Recovery Services to offer on-site supportive services for individuals and families experiencing or at risk of homelessness.</p><p>The nearly $35 million project was supported by $4.2 million in tax increment financing and $540,000 in Chicago Recovery Plan Permanent Supportive Housing funds. The Illinois Housing Development Authority, Federal Home Loan Bank’s Affordable Housing Program and ComEd were also among the financial supporters.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div eighth project in Illinois. Gorman has completed more than 20 school-to-apartment conversion projects, with market-rate and affordable units. Its next project, Regenerator, is in partnership with local community groups and will turn West Englewood's former Woods Mathematics and Science Academy into a community and health center with affordable housing. And Gorman's redevelopment proposal for the former Bontemps Elementary School is pending city approvals, according to the city.</p><p>The Earle building is 129 years old and on the National Register of Historic Places. It served students for more than a century before it became <a class="Link" href="https://graphics.suntimes.com/education/2023/chicagos-50-closed-schools/" target="_blank" >one of 50 Chicago schools to close</a> under then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel. Some of the shuttered schools have been converted into other uses, including luxury, low-income or senior apartments. But a 2023 Sun-Times and WBEZ investigation found the majority remain vacant.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson, who was a Chicago Teachers Union organizer when Charles Warrington closed, reflected on the school closure's impact. He said Wednesday that he fought against the city's school closures because he “knew the damage that it would cause.”</p><p>“I am so honored to be standing in the community that I organized to protect,” Johnson said. “Now, I get to cut the ribbon at a school that was closed, bringing affordable housing as mayor of the city of Chicago.”</p><p>Charles Mayfield, chief operating office of Chicago Public Schools, said CPS is “hyperfocused” on forging partnerships to bring buildings like Earle back to community use. He said the Chicago Board of Education recently approved the sale of more former school buildings for reuse, with another round of sales to come “in the weeks ahead.”</p><p>“Even when transformation takes a long time, it's still worth pursuing,” Mayfield said. “Look at Gorman & Co. and the Phoenix Foundation and this coalition of partners have done here. It's magical, it's beautiful and they didn't erase Earle's history. They preserved it.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/10/02/englewood-shuttered-charles-warrington-earle-school-gorman-affordable-apartment-community" >Englewood’s shuttered Charles Warrington Earle School getting new life as affordable apartment community</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Jordan Love has Packers' offense clicking, and better chance at 70% than Bears' Caleb Williams
entries.summary: <p>GREEN BAY, Wis. — I know, I know; we’re talking about practice.</p><p>But, man, for the Packers’ offense, that was some practice.</p><p>“We started off the day really hot,” quarterback Jordan Love said.</p><p>Indeed they did. In their joint practice Wednesday with the Cardinals, Love connected with his top three wide receivers: Matthew Golden, Jayden Reed and Christian Watson. The passes were on target, the timing was perfect and the plays were big. The quartet is set to explode.</p><p>The completions brought to mind Bears coach Ben Johnson’s goal — no, mandate — for Caleb Williams to complete 70% of his passes. After Williams finished last among 24 qualified quarterbacks in 2025 with a 58.1 completion percentage, that seems like a long shot.</p><p>For Love, it’s quite possible.</p><p>“Yeah, 70% completion percentage is attainable,” he said.</p><p>Coach Matt LaFleur agreed, but he isn’t pressing Love to reach it the way Johnson is with Williams. LaFleur said there’s more nuance to it.</p><p>“It’s all circumstantial in terms of what are we calling,” he said. “The deeper the concepts that you run, typically the lower the completion percentage, especially if you’re pushing the ball down the field. But that’s why as a quarterback, you have to make great decisions. If the deep ball’s not there, can you check it down and just keep the sticks moving?”</p><p>Said Love: “Completion percentage is one of those things you might look at after the game, at the end of the season. But it’s not something you’re focused on throughout the game. The goal is to improve that every year and have a great completion percentage. I’m not even sure what I was at last year.”</p><p>He was at 66.3%, 11th in the league among qualified QBs. The Patriots’ Drake Maye led the way at 72%; he was the only one to break 70%. And Love indeed improved on his first two full seasons at the helm.</p><p>Williams went the other way in his second full season. Yet, he has built so much excitement from his improbable fourth-quarter comebacks that he’s on the cover of the video game Madden NFL 27. Meanwhile, without such balleyhoo and drama, Love carries on.</p><p>“For me, it’s just about continuing to keep my head down and do my job,” he said when asked about Williams’ comparative rise in fame. “Focus on what we’re doing here in this building and try to lead this team to be the best team we can be.”</p><p>Love will face some challenges, starting with the offensive line. Jordan Morgan, the Packers’ first-round pick in 2024, is taking over at left tackle. Sean Rhyan is doing the same at center, where he barely played before being thrust into the position because of an injury last year.</p><p>Running back Josh Jacobs participated in the scrimmage with the Cardinals, but he’s facing a potential suspension from the NFL after being arrested on domestic-violence charges, including strangulation and suffocation. Turning to little-used MarShawn Lloyd would be a big comedown.</p><p>“I’m pretty confident we can sustain it,” general manager Brian Gutekunst said. “We’ll deal with that when that comes, but we’ve obviously been preparing for that in case that happens. I feel really good about the guys we’ve got in that room.”</p><p>The defense might not have star edge rusher Micah Parsons, who’s recovering from a torn anterior cruciate ligament, until Week 5, which happens to be the first matchup with the Bears. Parsons is the first player in NFL history with at least 12 sacks in each of his first five seasons.</p><p>“There’s not many Micah Parsons on the planet,” Gutekunst said. “There’s only so many guys in our game that can affect the game the way he does.”</p><p>Love is turning into that type of player, as he demonstrated on Ray Nitschke Field. But he wasn’t happy with how the offense ended the practice, which he certainly would say about the way the Packers ended last season.</p><p>The Packers were 9-3-1 and led the Broncos by nine in the third quarter. They lost by eight, setting off a skid that lasted the rest of the season. The Packers lost their final four regular-season games, then blew a 21-6 fourth-quarter lead to the Bears in the playoffs.</p><p>For all of Love’s success in the regular season, the Packers have earned the seventh and final NFC playoff seed in each of his three seasons since taking over for Aaron Rodgers — and they have one postseason victory to show for it.</p><p>Granted, we’re only talking about practice, but this season might end differently.</p>
